steps.editorState:
How to play - friendly game

  1. Player 1 rolls the dice.
  2. They write the number in any square on their grid.
  3. Then Player 2 rolls the dice.
  4. Players keep taking turns until the grids are full.
  5. Players read the numbers aloud.
  6. The winner has the biggest number.

How to play - nasty game

  1. Players take turns to roll the dice.
  2. This time they can write the numbers on their own grid or the other player's grid.

steps.text: How do maths games help with learning?

steps.editorState:
Fun

Games can be an enjoyable, motivating way to practice a skill many times.

Positive feelings

Having fun together encourages positive feelings towards maths and can reduce worry about making mistakes.

Memory

Skills that are practiced when a child is fully engaged and relaxed are more likely to be remembered.

Number sense

In trying to win, children really think about the numbers they choose. This builds number sense - a deeper, more flexible understanding of numbers.

Problem solving

Finding strategies to win develops problem solving skills.

Mathematical Vocabulary

Talking about a game or explaining it to someone else encourages children to use mathematical vocabulary.

Deeper thinking

Changing a rule and talking about how that impacts a game encourages an even deeper level of thinking.

Kitchen Safety

steps.editorState:
Cooking is great fun for children, but remember to talk to them about how to stay safe in the kitchen. Adults should always supervise children when cooking.

Safety rules might include:

  • Always ask an adult before you cook.
  • Ask an adult if you need boiling water or a hot oven.
  • Ask an adult to supervise when you use a knife.
  • Move carefully in the kitchen - don't run around.
  • Wipe up any spills straight away so noone slips.

Hygiene rules might include:

  • Wash your hands with soap and water.
  • Wipe down work surfaces before you start.
  • Tie back long hair and wear and apron if you have one.
  • If you lick your fingers, wash your hands again.
  • Keep cooked and uncooked food separate. Be especially careful with raw meat and fish.
  • Ask an adult to check everything is properly cooked before you eat it.

steps.text: The Solution

steps.editorState:
6004-3214 = 2790

So Jamie had to give 2790 doubloons to the trolls

Solution

2 x 1000 doubloon coins to the biggest troll. (2000)

7 x 100 doubloon coins to the middle troll (700)

9 x 10 doubloon coins to the last troll. (90)

There are other ways to solve it as well.

Setting out:

Jamie was going on an adventure in a land that used gold coins.

The coins in this land were worth either 1, 10, 100 or 1000 doubloons. 

Jamie had coins in her purse that were worth 6004 doubloons.

The journey:

She came to three bridges that she needed to cross but each one was guarded by a troll who demanded a toll. A toll is a cost to cross the bridge.

The first troll demanded to be paid in coins worth 1000 doubloons each.

The second troll demanded to be paid in coins each worth 100 doubloons.

The third troll demanded to be paid in coins each worth 10 doubloons.

The end:

By the time Jamie had paid the tolls and crossed all three bridges she had coins left that were worth 3214 gold doubloons.

How many coins did each troll take?

steps.text: How do maths games help with learning?

steps.editorState:
Fun

Games can be an enjoyable, motivating way to practice a skill many times.

Positive feelings

Having fun together encourages positive feelings towards maths and can reduce worry about making mistakes.

Memory

Skills that are practiced when a child is fully engaged and relaxed are more likely to be remembered.

Number sense

In trying to win, children really think about the numbers they choose. This builds number sense - a deeper, more flexible understanding of numbers.

Problem solving

Finding strategies to win develops problem solving skills.

Mathematical Vocabulary

Talking about a game or explaining it to someone else encourages children to use mathematical vocabulary.

Deeper thinking

Changing a rule and talking about how that impacts a game encourages an even deeper level of thinking.

Teaching your child to tell the time

steps.editorState:
Learning to tell the time is tricky.

Children need lots of practice and lots of repetition.

Parents are the ideal people to help children learn as they are with children through more times of the day.

  • Use the time when you are talking to your children. For example 'we'll have tea at 6 o'clock' or 'You can play on the computer until half past five then its time to stop'. 
  • Point out the time as part of your routine - Its 7 o'clock. Its bedtime' or 'Its half past eight, we need to get going'.
  • Practice reading the time on different clocks you see out and about.
  • Work up slowly - start with o'clock times, then half past, then the quarter hour.
  • Use analogue clocks until children are confident, then start to talk about digital time too.

Top Tip: If you don't have an analogue clock at home, you can change the clock on your mobile phone to analogue.

steps.text: The aim of this game is to be the player with the smallest remainder at the end! Roll the dice below to generate a 4-digit number.

Now that you have a four-digit number, each player chooses a number between 3 and 9. All players use short division to divide the four-digit number by their number between 3 and 9.

The player with the smallest remainder wins, as long as their calculation is correct!

You will need to find some small objects from your kitchen (e.g. a spoon, a tin of beans etc.).

Give the other person two objects. They hold them in their hands and decide which is heaviest and which is lightest

For a challenge you can order several objects from heaviest to lightest.

Do some baking together! It can be anything you like as long as you are measuring the mass of the ingredients together.

Stuck for ideas? Try these easy rock buns!

100g margarine/butter
200g self-raising flour
1 tsp cinnamon
1 tsp baking powder
85g soft brown sugar
100g sultanas
1 egg


Recipe:

1. Heat oven to 180°C/160°C fan/gas mark 4.
2. Grease a baking tray.
3. Mix the flour, baking powder and cinnamon in a bowl. Add the butter/margarine and rub into the mixture until you have something that looks like fine breadcrumbs.
4. Stir in the fruit and sugar and then add the milk and egg.
5. Mix to a firm dough.
6. Spoon 10 rough blobs of the mixture onto the baking tray, leaving some room in between for spreading whilst cooking.
7. Bake for 20-25 minutes until golden brown.
Kitchen Safety

steps.editorState:
Cooking is great fun for children, but remember to talk to them about how to stay safe in the kitchen. Adults should always supervise children when cooking.

Safety rules might include:

  • Always ask an adult before you cook.
  • Ask an adult if you need boiling water or a hot oven.
  • Ask an adult to supervise when you use a knife.
  • Move carefully in the kitchen - don't run around.
  • Wipe up any spills straight away so noone slips.

Hygiene rules might include:

  • Wash your hands with soap and water.
  • Wipe down work surfaces before you start.
  • Tie back long hair and wear and apron if you have one.
  • If you lick your fingers, wash your hands again.
  • Keep cooked and uncooked food separate. Be especially careful with raw meat and fish.
  • Ask an adult to check everything is properly cooked before you eat it.

steps.text: Rules

steps.editorState:
The aim of the game:

To make a chosen total by sliding the counter around the board, adding on numbers as you go.

The winner is the one who makes the move that reaches the total.


How to play:

1. Choose a target to reach. This is the total both of you are trying to make.

2. Player 1 places their counter on the game board over one of the numbers and says that number.

3. Player 2 moves the same counter in any direction along a line to a number and says the total of the two numbers.

4. Player 1 moves the same counter to cover another neighbouring number, adds on that number, and says the 'running' total of the three numbers.

5. Keep sliding and adding until the total is reached.

6. Players must move when it is their turn.

7. No 'jumping' is allowed.

8. If you go over the target number, you've lost!

How to play:
Your target number is 50. This is the total that both players are trying to make.

Player 1 rolls the dice above. They can choose whether to double the number shown or halve the number shown.

Player 2 rolls the dice. In the same way, they choose whether to double the number shown or halve the number shown. Player 2 adds their number onto Player 1's number to make a running total.

Play continues like this with each player rolling the dice, halving or doubling the number and adding the result onto the running total.

The winner is the player who reaches the target exactly.

Now, have another go using a different target number.

steps.text: Playdough Recipe

steps.editorState:
Ingredients:

  • 1 cup plain flour 
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil (baby oil and coconut oil work too) 
  • 1/4 cup salt 
  • 1 tablespoon cream of tartar 
  • 0.5-0.75 cups boiling water (adding in increments until it feels just right) 
  • food colouring (optional) 
  • few drops glycerine (the secret ingredient for extra stretch and shine) (optional) 
  • a sealable bag or box to keep the play dough in when you have finished playing

steps.text: Boiling water safety

steps.editorState:
Method:

  1. Mix the flour, salt, cream of tartar and oil in a mixing bowl. 
  2. Add the foodcolouring (if you are using it) to the hot water and then tip some of the water into the dry ingredients. 
  3. Stir continuously until it becomes a sticky, combined dough, adding more water if it is too dry. 
  4. Add the glycerine, if you are using it. 
  5. Allow it to cool down then take it out of the bowl and knead it vigorously for a couple of minutes until all of the stickiness has gone. The kneading is really important because it's what makes the dough lovely and stretchy. 
  6. If it is still a little sticky then add a bit more flour until it is just right! 
  7. Your playdough is ready to use!
This no-cook recipe should take you about four minutes to make and keep for around six months! Of course, you could use another recipe or play dough you have bought from a shop instead.

  5. Allow it to cool down then take it out of the bowl and knead it vigorously for a couple of minutes until all of the stickiness has gone. The kneading is really important because it's what makes the dough lovely and stretchy. 
  6. If it is still a little sticky then add a bit more flour until it is just right! 
  7. Your playdough is ready to use!

steps.text: Playdough recipe
Boiling water safety

steps.editorState:
Method:

  1. Mix the flour, salt, cream of tartar and oil in a mixing bowl. 
  2. Add the foodcolouring (if you are using it) to the hot water and then tip some of the water into the dry ingredients. 
  3. Stir continuously until it becomes a sticky, combined dough, adding more water if it is too dry. 
  4. Add the glycerine, if you are using it. 
  5. Allow it to cool down then take it out of the bowl and knead it vigorously for a couple of minutes until all of the stickiness has gone. The kneading is really important because it's what makes the dough lovely and stretchy. 
  6. If it is still a little sticky then add a bit more flour until it is just right! 
  7. Your playdough is ready to use!
This no-cook recipe should take you about four minutes to make and keep for around six months! Of course, you could use another recipe or play dough you have bought from a shop instead.

Ingredients:

  • 1 cup plain flour 
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil (baby oil and coconut oil work too) 
  • 1/4 cup salt 
  • 1 tablespoon cream of tartar 
  • 0.5-0.75 cups boiling water (adding in increments until it feels just right) 
  • food colouring (optional) 
  • few drops glycerine (the secret ingredient for extra stretch and shine) (optional) 
  • a sealable bag or box to keep the play dough in when you have finished playing

You will need:

Blue tack, plasticine or play dough. You can make your own play dough using the recipe below.

This no-cook recipe should take you about four minutes to make and keep for around six months! Of course, you could use another recipe or play dough you have bought from a shop instead.

Ingredients:

  • 1 cup plain flour 
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil (baby oil and coconut oil work too) 
  • 1/4 cup salt 
  • 1 tablespoon cream of tartar 
  • 0.5-0.75 cups boiling water (adding in increments until it feels just right) 
  • food colouring (optional) 
  • few drops glycerine (the secret ingredient for extra stretch and shine) (optional) 
  • a sealable bag or box to keep the play dough in when you have finished playing

Kitchen Safety

steps.editorState:
Cooking is great fun for children, but remember to talk to them about how to stay safe in the kitchen. Adults should always supervise children when cooking.

Safety rules might include:

  • Always ask an adult before you cook.
  • Ask an adult if you need boiling water or a hot oven.
  • Ask an adult to supervise when you use a knife.
  • Move carefully in the kitchen - don't run around.
  • Wipe up any spills straight away so noone slips.

Hygiene rules might include:

  • Wash your hands with soap and water.
  • Wipe down work surfaces before you start.
  • Tie back long hair and wear and apron if you have one.
  • If you lick your fingers, wash your hands again.
  • Keep cooked and uncooked food separate. Be especially careful with raw meat and fish.
  • Ask an adult to check everything is properly cooked before you eat it.

Setting up:

Do this without your child.

You will need:
  • 3 boxes (different sizes)
  • 3 objects to put in the boxes
  • Tape (optional)


What to do:
  1. Find three boxes.
  2. Put an object inside each box.
  3. Close the boxes so you can't see what is inside!

Top tip:
When you choose your objects, pick things with interesting weights, that make a sound inside the box, or that move in interesting ways when you tip the box.

The activity:

Now show your child the boxes!

  1. What could be in the first box?
    Don't touch it yet!
  2. Does the size of the box give you any clues?
    Think of several ideas. Think of some things it definitely couldn't be!
  3. Pick up the box. Hold it still and feel the weight.
    Does this change what you think it could be? Is there anything else you now know it can't be?
  4. Give the box a little shake.
    Can you hear anything that gives you a clue?
  5. Use all your senses to guess what could be in the box.
    Choose three things it could be, and then choose one to be your final guess.
  6. Open the box to see if you were right!
    Did you guess anything that was nearly right? Is there anything you felt or heard that gave you a really good clue?
  7. Repeat the activity with the other boxes.
    Use what you learned from the first box to help you work out the others!

Practise:

  1. Practise saying the words.
    It will be better if you know the words off by heart because then you can concentrate on the performance.
  2. Think about how to turn it into a performance.
    • Speak (or sing) loudly and clearly (but without shouting);
    • Stand up tall to show you are ready to perform;
    • Think about any actions you could include.
  3. Practise your performace.
    Go through it five or six times so that you are really confident with what you are doing.


Perform:

  1. Find an audience.
    It could be one person, it could be your whole family, or you could even record your performance.
  2. Perform your nursery rhyme.
    You could even take a bow when the audience is clapping!
Choose a nursery rhyme you would like to perform. It could be one from the orange button below, one you already know, or a new one you would like to learn!

You will need:

An ordinary household object. In the example, it is a wooden spoon, but you could choose anything!

How to play:

In this game, the object is allowed to be anything apart from itself. So if you are using a spoon, it can be anything apart from a spoon.

  1. Player 1 holds the spoon and pretends it is something else. For example, they could brush their hair with it.
  2. Player 2 tries to guess what the spoon is being. Is it a shower? Is it a hair brush?
  3. When they have guessed, Player 2 takes the spoon and pretends it is something else.
  4. Keep taking it in turns with the spoon. See how many different things it can be!
Dressing up clothes ideas
It can actually be better if you don't have any specific character "outfits" because then it is easier to imagine being anything you choose!
Box filled with dressing up clothes

Some people will already have a dressing up box, but if you don't, don't worry! It is possible to make a really fun dressing up box from things you already have in the house. Here are some ideas:

  • Scarves
  • Hats
  • An old pair of shoes
  • An old bag
  • A big t-shirt
  • A belt or ribbon
  • Necklaces
  • An old net curtain
  • Sunglasses

In this activity, you are going to pretend to be characters from a story. Pretending to be characters helps children think about the story in more depth, particularly about the characters, their feelings, and why they acted the way they did.

How to play:

  1. Choose a character each from a story. You could be from the same story or different stories, either is fun (though the same story is easier to start with).
  2. Dress up as your characters (dressing up clothes ideas below).
  3. Play together as your characters. This could be:
    • Acting out part of the story together;
    • Pretend to go on an adventure together in the garden;
    • Build a den together;
    • Have a pretend tea party;
    • Do an ordinary household activity but as your characters, e.g. setting the table for dinner.


Let your child take the lead and see where they take you!

How to play:

Discuss one of the 'would you rather' questions together.

steps.text: More question suggestions

steps.editorState:
Would you rather...

  • always be ten minutes late or twenty minutes early?
  • be able to fly or be able to turn invisible?
  • not be allowed to watch TV for a year or not eat sweets for a year?
  • sweat honey or always smell like a skunk?
  • be as tall as a house or as small as a mouse?
  • have hands instead of feet or a tail?
  • be able to see through walls or read people’s minds?
  • eat ice cream for every meal or never eat ice cream again?
  • be itchy for the rest of your life or sticky for the rest of your life?
  • travel back in time or into the future?

There is no "right" answer to these questions, so your discussion should last several minutes, as you try to work out what you think, explain your reasons, and work out what might make you choose the other option. Both people should share their ideas!

With your child, discuss who would win if there was a battle:

Example first sentence

You could start out by thinking of a story you know, but because you are only saying one word at a time, it can soon change into something else! The real challenge is just going with where the other person takes you, even if it wasn't what you imagined would come next!

How to play:

Take it in turns to say a word to tell a story.

Aim of the game:

In this storytelling game, one person keeps making things go wrong and the other person keeps trying to fix it!

How to play:

Choose who is Player 1 - they fix the problems. Player 2 makes things go wrong!

  1. Player 1 starts with the opening sentence of a story, e.g. 'One day Jessie went to the park.'
  2. Player 2 begins their sentence with the word unfortunately and makes everything go wrong, for example, 'Unfortunately, there was a tiger sitting on the swing.'
  3. Player 1 begins their sentence with the word fortunately and tries to fix the problem, for example, 'Fortunately, the tiger was not hungry today.'
  4. Keep taking it in turns to add to the story and see what happens!
Folded and decorated fortune teller
Make your own fortune teller

Draw in Your Fortune Teller:

Inside the fortune teller, you need to draw some pictures:
  • The outer layer is four main characters;
  • The middle layer is eight possible problems;
  • The inner layer is eight possible endings.
Instructions for how to fold a fortune teller
Fold Your Fortune Teller:
Illustrated fortune teller laid flat and folded into shape
For this activity, you will need a folded fortune teller. You can either make your own using our instructions or print one which is already decorated.

How to play:

  1. Choose a character from the outside layer.
  2. Begin telling your story.
  3. When you get to the point that you need a problem, spell out the name of your character as you open and close the fortune teller to choose which inner section you will be looking at.
  4. When you are looking at the inner section, choose your problem.
  5. Keep telling the story.
  6. When you get to the point that you need a solution to the problem, choose a flap to open and find out your solution.
  7. Finish telling your story!


Have a few goes - your storytelling skills will improve as you tell more stories!

Ideas of everyday tasks:

  • Putting on a hat, scarf and gloves;
  • Making a sandwich;
  • Running the bath;
  • Putting on your shoes;
  • Making a cup of tea.

How to play:

You are going to be a robot and your child is going to program you to carry out an everyday task. They will give you instructions and you should follow them exactly. The instructions may not work! Your child might need to change what they are saying to help you to complete the task!
For this activity you will need an object or a picture.

The activity:

  1. Tell your child that you've found this interesting thing or picture and you want to chat about it.
  2. Begin by saying "I notice…" and completing the sentence with something you notice, e.g. if it is a sieve, "I notice it has lots of little holes in it."
  3. Ask what they notice, and encourage them to start their answer with "I notice".
  4. You could do a couple of things you notice each.
  5. Repeat with "I think" and "I wonder".


Note:

I notice is things you can see (or feel or smell or hear).
I think is ideas you have about it and things you can work out.
I wonder is things you want to know or are not sure about.
Object and picture suggestions
A newspaper and magazine stand, a shelf of books, and old photographs.

Here are some ideas of objects and pictures you could use:

Object:

You can use any object, from something really every-day like a shoe to something more mysterious like the rattle in the video. It could be something from in your house like a mug or something you have found when out on a walk like a leaf. You might be able to pick it up like a pine cone or it might be enormous like a tree. You can choose anything!
A pine cone, a mug, a tree and a paperclip.

Picture:

You can use any picture. It could be in a book or in a newspaper, it could be an advert or an illustration, it could be in a story you are reading together or it could be a photo in an information book. You can choose anything!

steps.text:
How to play:

Take it in turns to describe an object in the room without naming it. Try to include as much detail as you can to help them. Can the other person guess what it is?

Tips:

  • Use adjectives (describing words) for its colour, texture, shape and size;
  • Describe where it is in relation to other things, for instance 'behind the sofa' or 'near the window';
  • If you point or look at the object, it will be too easy!

You will need:

  • Paper
  • Something to draw with

How to play:

  1. Roll the die to choose a picture. Do not show it to the other person.
  2. Describe it for the other person to draw. Try to describe the shapes rather than naming the parts, e.g. 'Draw a rectangle in the middle' not 'Draw a door'.
  3. Try not to look at their picture while they are drawing it.
  4. When they have finished, look at what they have drawn and show them the picture.
  5.  Did they draw it right? How could you have described it better?
  6. Swap over so that the other person has a go at describing.

steps.text:
Setting up:

  1. Cut or tear your paper into about 24 pieces large enough to write a word on.
  2. Write a noun on each piece of paper.
  3. Fold each piece of paper and put it into your container.

You will need:

  • A piece of paper;
  • Something to write with;
  • A two minute timer (maybe the one on your phone);
  • A hat (or other similar sized container).
What words should we write?

In this game, we are describing nouns, so all your words need to be nouns. For example:
  • Cat
  • Chair
  • Rhys Stevenson
  • Grandma
  • A carrot

It's also really important that both players can read all the words!

If you're still stuck for ideas, you could print the sheet of words below or copy some of them onto your own paper. They are all short words that should be simple for your child to read.

How to play:

  1. Choose who is going to describe first. This is Player 1.
  2. Start the two minute timer.
  3. Player 1 must describe as many words as they can to Player 2 before the time runs out. You must not say the word or its spelling!
  4. Each time Player 2 correctly guesses a word, Player 1 keeps the paper (so you can see how many you successfully described).
  5. When the time runs out, swap over so Player 2 can describe some words.
  6. Keep swapping over until all the words have run out.
  7. Count up the number of words each person successfully described. Who described the most? They are the winner!

steps.editorState:
Before you start:

Look at your emotions cards. Go through them together and work out what different emotions they all show.

steps.text:
You will need:

Emotions cards. Click below to download if they have not been sent home.
A grid of koala faces with different expressions.

How to play:

  1. Put the cards in a pile.
    Make sure the pile is face down so you can't see what is on them.
  2. Turn over the top card.
    Do it secretly so the other person can't see.
  3. Act out the emotion on the card.
    Use your face, body and voice.
  4. Can the other person guess which emotion you are showing?
    Act some more if you need to!
  5. Swap over to let the other person have a go.
    Take it in turns until all the cards have gone.
The aim of the game is to ask lots of questions and make the other person laugh! It can be good to practise each type of question before you start.

steps.editorState:
How to play:

  • Player 1 asks questions.
  • Player 2 answers the questions (using the answers above). 
  • Player 2 must not laugh! 
  • If Player 2 does laugh, swap over so Player 2 is now asking the questions.

steps.text:
The questions:


Horace's Cat:
If you are asked a question and the answer is a person or an animal you must say 'Horace's Cat'.

Yes/no:
If you are asked a question and the answer is 'yes' you must say 'no'.
If you are asked a question and the answer is 'no' you must say 'yes'.

Cucumbers:
If you are asked a question and the answer is anything else you must say 'Cucumbers'.

Some suggestions of jobs:

Firefighter, pilot, farmer, shop keeper, musician, police officer, doctor, teacher, scientist, writer, builder, computer programmer, cleaner, sailor, vet, waiter, actor, plumber...

steps.text:
How to play:

  1. Choose a job. Don't tell the other person what it is!
  2. They ask questions to work out what your job is. It is better if they have yes/no answers.
  3. When they have guessed what your job is, swap over so you get a chance to ask the questions.
  4. Keep taking it in turns to choose a job.

The aim of the game:

To think about different ways you can do actions, e.g. 'quietly', 'angrily' or 'excitedly'.

How to play:

  1. Player 1 chooses an action and mimes doing it (acts it out without talking). For example, you could mime putting on a hat.
  2. Player 2 guesses what Player 1 is doing.
  3. Player 1 does the action again but changes how they are doing it, e.g. you could be putting on your hat angrily.
  4. Player 2 guesses how Player 1 is doing the action,
  5. When Player 2 has guessed how Player 1 is doing the action, swap over.
  6. Player 2 repeats the game from step 1.
  7. Take it in turns to have some more goes!


Roll the die for some ideas of how to change your actions:

steps.text:
How to play:

Give both players a piece of paper. You are going to be drawing a monster each!

  1. Fold the paper into three to make one section for the head, one for the body and one for the legs.
  2. Draw a monster's head in the top section of your paper. Make it as crazy or as fierce as you like! Don't show the other person what you have drawn!
  3. Fold over the paper so that the monster's head is hidden. Make sure the neck lines are still poking out!
  4. Swap paper with the other person and draw a body onto their head (you can't look what their head is like).
  5. Fold over the paper so that the monster's body is hidden. Make sure the waist lines are still poking out!
  6. Swap paper again and draw legs onto the monster.
  7. Fold over the paper so the whole monster is hidden.
  8. Swap paper again and open up the paper to see what your monster is like!
  9. Describe your monster to the other person - what is it like?

Challenge:

Choose a name for your monster and write it at the top of the paper. Then write descriptive phrases around your monster to show what it is like!

You will need:

  • Paper;
  • Colouring pencils or pens;
  • A writing pen or pencil.
Monster drawing with words to describe it written around, e.g. 'silly' and 'naughty'.
Overhead view of two children drawing monsters onto folded paper
Choose a book your child has not read before.You could do this with a book your child is reading, or one you are reading to them.

Before you read: look at the front cover


  1. What do you think will happen in the story?
    This is your prediction.
  2. What clues helped you make your prediction?
    Talk about what clues you can see, including the title and pictures.


During reading: stop and talk


  1. What might happen next?
    They might just guess, but encourage them to try using what they have already read to help.
  2. You could show them (model) how to use clues in the book to make a better prediction.
    Try asking questions as part of your model to get your child to add their own ideas, e.g. "That's interesting, I was thinking about how he found a key on the last page. I wonder what the key could be for? Do you think he might use it on the next page?"
  3. Carry on reading. Was your prediction correct?
    Remember, you don't need to be exactly right, as long as you had a thoughtful idea about what might happen. Sometimes authors like to surprise you!
  4. Stop and make more predictions later in the book.
    Can you use what you found out after your first prediction to help you this time?


After reading: challenge

What might happen if there was another book after this one?

For this activity, you will need to walk somewhere. In the video below, they use a mini figure and a drawn scene, but it is much more fun if you are actually walking about! You could do the activity while you are walking around the house, or on the way to school or the shops.

Challenge:

Try adding adjectives (describing words) e.g. "up the steep stairs".

How to play:

Walk somewhere, and while you are walking, say where you're moving, e.g.:
  • Up the stairs;
  • Across the road;
  • Into a puddle.

Challenge:

You could also try this activity with imaginary maps! Perhaps you could do a map to show Little Red Riding Hood how to get to Grandma's house, or one for Hansel and Gretel to find their way home. Let your imagination go wild!

You will need:

Paper and pencils or pens.

The activity:

  1. Draw a map of your journey to school. Include pictures of things you walk past, under, across etc.
  2. While you are drawing, talk about where you would be walking and the things you walk past, under and across etc.
  3. When you have finished drawing, write instructions of how to get to school. Use the things from steps one and two to help describe what to do, e.g. "First, walk across the road."

Thinking of lots of words which mean the same thing is really useful because it can help make your speaking and your writing more interesting. It can also help you understand what you are reading!

Here are some more words it could be fun to think about:
How many words can you think of that mean 'big'?

steps.text:
You can probably come up with loads of your own!

Challenge:

Make a little booklet and write your starting word at the top of the page. You can then make a list of all the synonyms (words which mean the same thing) underneath. If you do this with several words, you have made your own thesaurus. A thesaurus is a special book which has lists of words which mean the same thing. You could add words into your thesaurus when you hear them or find them in your reading!

Get creative! Think about these questions together:

The activity:

Work together to retell a story you know.

Ideas:

Here are some ways you could retell the story:
  • Say the words, taking it in turns to add the next part of the story;
  • Use mini-figures to act out the story;
  • Make little puppets to help you;
  • Use the pictures in a book but use your own words;
  • Some children's books have a story map in the back to use for retelling stories;
  • Draw your own story map (see example above).

Challenge:

Turn your story into a book! Fold your book using the instructions below, then write the story onto the pages inside. You could also think of a title to write on the front of your book! Don't forget to add illustrations (pictures).
The simplest story has five parts:

steps.text: For this activity, you will need a story bag. It can be any bag you have in the house, though it's better if it's not see-through!

The activity:

When you have filled your bag, the storytelling can begin!

You can use the bag in any way you like, but here are some ideas you could choose from:

  • Choose an object to be the main character in your story;
  • Start telling a story and pull out an object to help you decide what happens next (like in the video below);
  • You could take out all the objects at once and use them to set up a story scene;
  • Retell a story you know, but swap the objects in the story for things in the bag and see what happens;
  • Choose three things from the bag and create a story which uses all three.
Filling Your bag

You need to choose about ten things to put in your bag. They can be any small objects from around the house which could be used in the story. Children have amazing imaginations, so you can choose almost anything!

Here are some ideas:
  • A piece of jewellery
  • Ribbon
  • A pebble
  • A comb
  • A coin
  • A button
  • A plastic animal
  • A spoon
  • A piece of pasta
  • An elastic band
  • A toy car

The activity:

Read the book together. Stop on a page and talk about what the character is feeling or why they did what they did. Look at the pictures and the words to find clues to help you work it out.

You can try again on other pages in the book!

You will need:

A book. It can be one your child is able to read themself, or it can be one you are reading to them!

How to play:

  1. Choose a character from a story each.
    They do not have to be from the same story!
  2. Pretend to be your character.
    Dressing up as them can really help!
  3. Choose who is the host of the party.
    It can be easier if this is the grownup.
  4. The host welcomes the guest to the party.
    Remember to keep being the characters!
  5. Have a conversation about your days.
    Make sure you ask each other about how you were feeling at different points in your stories!


You can play this game at any time. You could pretend to be characters from a story when you are eating dinner, running the bath or in the car on the way to school!
Role play is a really good way of thinking about the feelings of characters in stories.

Aim of the game:

To take it in turns to add items to a list, using 'and' before the last item.

Challenge:

Try adding things in alphabetical order (e.g. an apple, three bananas, a chair, a dog basket etc.). If you are really good at your alphabet, it might actually make it easier to remember more things!

How to play:

  1. One person starts by saying 'When I went to market, I bought...' and choosing one item they could buy.
  2. The other person repeats what the first person has said, using 'and' to add the last item.
  3. The first person then repeats what the second person has said, again adding an extra item at the end of the list. Make sure you only say 'and' before the last item in the list! (The mum in the video is doing this.)
  4. Keep taking it in turns to add something until it is too hard to remember the whole list!
Example Market Game

Adult: When I went to market, I bought a cake.
Child: When I went to market, I bought a cake and some apples.
Adult: When I went to market, I bought a cake, some apples and a bath towel.
Child: When I went to market, I bought a cake, some apples, a bath towel and three balloons.
Adult: When I went to market, I bought a cake, some apples, a bath towel, three balloons and a cruise ship.

You will need:

  • A tray (or you can just play at the table);
  • About twenty small objects that you can put on the tray;
  • A teatowel or other cloth that can cover the objects
Tray with lots of objects: a toothbrush, toothpaste, pasta, spoon, rubber, car, peg, plaster, chopstick, pencil, crayon, straw, elastic band, wooden horse, tape measure, coin, candle and cotton wool.

How to play:

  1. Spread the objects out on the tray so that you can see them all.
  2. Look at all the objects together and check you both know what they all are.
  3. Cover the tray with a towel and remove two objects (secretly so the other player does not see).
  4. Uncover the tray.
  5. Ask the other player to guess which two objects have been removed. They should say the two objects connected with and, e.g. 'I think the fork and the pencil are missing.'
  6. When they have guessed, put the objects back and play again.

steps.text:
The activity:

Look at the piece of writing together and ask these questions:

  1. Can you find a sentence?

  2. How do you know where it starts and ends?
    • It starts with a capital letter.
    • It ends with a full stop, exclamation mark or question mark.

  3. Why did the writer put the punctuation there?
    • To help you read the sentence easily;
    • To help you understand what the writing means;
    • In this piece of writing, they ended the sentence here because...


The adult can read the words to aid discussion, but do point to the words as you read aloud so that your child can see!

You will need:

A piece of writing with sentences on it.

It could be your child's reading book, a picture book you are sharing together, a magazine or even a cereal box. Just make sure you check that the sentences have capital letters at the start and full stops, exclamation marks or question marks at the end!

Here are some things you could change:
  • Try varying how you say the sentence (e.g. loud, quiet, happy, sad).
  • Try varying how long or complex the sentence is.
  • Add words to your first sentence and say totally different sentences!
  • Your child could have a go at making you copy, though the real focus is getting them to repeat a range of different sentences.

How to play:

Say a sentence and ask your child to repeat it. Then try changing your sentence!
You can let it get as silly as you like, as long as the sentences make sense!

How to play:

Take it in turns to say a word to build a silly sentence. If you get to the end of the sentence, shout "full stop" instead of saying a word.
<center>I / love / sprinkling / strawberries / on / my / pizza / full stop.</center>

steps.text: Example:

Things to look out for:

  • Children often get muddled in the middle of the alphabet with the letters l m n o p. Try to slow down their singing of this part so they really sound like separate letters and not one "lemonenopea"!
  • Try to encourage the British pronunciation of z 'zed' rather than the American z 'zee'.

The activity:

Sing the alphabet song together! You can use the video to help if you want!

The activity:

Work together to think of an animal beginning with each letter of the alphabet.

You can write down your ideas if you like, or just say the animals you think of!

Challenge:

Try adding adjectives when you think of your animals, e.g. amazing aardvarks, blue butterflies, cuddly cats etc.

Other things to try:

  • Make it competitive by taking it in turns to think of the next animal.
  • Add in actions as well as adjectives, e.g. acting with angry anteaters, bouncing with beautiful bees, etc.
  • Think of a different category instead of animals, e.g. foods.
  • Play in the car on a journey - you could make an alphabet of things you see out of the window.
How to make letter pegs

You will Need:

  • 26 pegs* (wooden are easiest to write on);
  • Two different coloured pens to write on the pegs.


What to Do:

1. On one side of each peg, write the alphabet using lower-case letters.
  • If you are only making one set of letters, make them lower-case because these are the most useful for reading and using when writing.
  • Write the vowels (a e i o u) in a different colour to show that these letters are special.

2. On the back of each peg, write the upper-case letter in the same colour.
  • Make sure the letter on the front of the peg is the same as the one on the back.
  • This will help practise seeing the difference between upper- and lower-case letters.

*NB: If you do not have 26 pegs, you can also make your own letter cards, or use magnetic letters you already have. The pegs are really good because you can build fine motor muscles at the same time, and because you can include upper- and lower-case letters, but anything with letters is a good way to practise the alphabet.

How to play:

  1. Mix up the pegs.
  2. Clip them onto the hanger in alphabetical order, using the lower case letters. Sing the alphabet song to help you if you need to!
  3. Did you spot any letters that were a different colour? These special letters are called vowels.
  4. Try again using the upper case letters.
  5. Which letters look similar in upper and lower case? Which look very different?

You will need:

  • 26 clothes pegs with lower-case letters written on (see instructions below)
  • A clothes hanger

Extra challenges:

  1. How fast can you clip the pegs in order onto the hanger?
  2. If your adult takes one peg away, can you spot what is missing?
  3. If you only have ten pegs, can you still put them in order? Did you leave the right space to add in the other pegs?
Child clipping pegs with letters onto a hanger in alphabetical order

How to play:

Tips for Clues:

Try to use a mix of clues! Ones about:
  • Spelling
    "It has an 'ur' sound in it," (Thursday) or "It has a silent letter in it," (Wednesday).
  • Activities you usually do on that day
    "We go to see Grandma," or "You have an after school club."
  • Its position in the week
    "It's a weekday" or "It comes after Tuesday."

How to play:

  1. Player 1 chooses an action beginning with 'un', e.g. 'unwrap'.
    You can use the list of suggestions to help if you like!
  2. Player 1 mimes the action.
    Act it out without saying anything!
  3. Player 2 guesses what the 'un' word is.
    They should say what it is then mime what it would look like without the 'un'.
  4. If Player 2 was correct, swap over.
    If they were incorrect, Player 1 does their mime again so Player 2 can have another guess.
  5. Keep playing until you have had a few goes each!

  4. Dress your adult up as the villain!

For this activity, you could use some dressing up clothes. You might have a favourite costume, but often the best dressing up can be scarves and old clothes from your wardrobe! Be as creative as you like!

steps.text:
How to play:

  1. Player 1 picks an animal. Don't say out loud what you have chosen!
  2. Player 1 describes the animal by saying what it does, e.g. 'It hops.' Try to give at least three clues.
  3. Player 2 must guess what it is.
  4. If Player 2 can't guess, Player 1 might need to give some extra clues.
  5. When Player 2 has guessed, swap over so they can give some clues.
  6. Repeat with six or more different animals.


Example:

Here are some example clues, with the important verbs (doing words) highlighted:
  • It jumps.
  • It sits on a log.
  • It catches flies.
  • It swims in a pond.
  • It croaks.
This activity is a really good way of practising using verbs (doing words) with 's' and 'es' endings.

How to Write Your Riddle:

  1. Think of an object, e.g. a spoon.
  2. Write three sentences that say what it does, e.g. 'It stirs,' or 'It mixes porridge.'
  3. Read each other's riddles and try to guess what they are!


Example Riddle:



What is it?
It opens.
It spins clothes round.
It makes things clean.
It is a washing machine!
Writing riddles can be really fun! Try one together to start with, and then have a go at writing them for each other to read and guess.

What to do:

  1. Player 1 chooses an object they can see.
  2. Player 1 says the object's name (e.g. "chairs") without using any extra words that might give away how many there are (not "a chair" or "a set of chairs").
  3. Player 2 says if there is one or more than one and how they know, e.g. "There is more than one chair because there was a 's' sound at the end."
  4. Try again with other objects you can see!
  5. Make sure you take turns so you can both have a go at hearing the different sounds!


Remember:

When there is more than one of something, the ending usually sounds different.
  • Sometimes the ending is 's', e.g. 'balls'.
  • Sometimes the ending is 'es' (which sounds like 'is'), e.g. 'foxes'.
My word changed in a different way...

Well done for spotting this!

Sometimes the ending might change in a different way, but we are mainly working on 's' and 'es'.

Sometimes the whole word can change (e.g. a 'tooth' and some 'teeth'), and sometimes it doesn't change at all (e.g. a 'sheep' and some 'sheep'). It is good to notice and talk about these too, but they are not the focus of this game.

steps.text:
Aim of the game:

Listen carefully to the end of a word to work out if it is singular or plural.

You can play this game anywhere! If you use a whole room, house, or even outside, you can use the objects you see around you (instead of setting it up at a table in advance).

How to play:

  1. Player 1 names an object(s) they can see, e.g. 'spades'.
  2. Player 2 listens carefully to the ending of the word:
    • If the word has s or es at the end, that means 'more than one'.
    • If the word has no extra ending, that means 'one'.
  3. Player 2 points at the object(s).
  4. Player 2 then says whether the word was singular or plural and how they knew.
  5. Take turns so you both get several goes at saying and hearing different endings.


Important:

You must only say a one-word clue. Say 'shoe' not 'a shoe' because the 'a' gives away that it is singular without having to listen to the end of the word.
Example Game

Player 1: "Shoes."
Player 2 points to two shoes.
Player 2: "I knew it was plural because you said 'shoes' not 'shoe'."
What do 'singular' and 'plural' mean?

Singular when the word is one of something, e.g. 'cat'.

Plural when the word is more than one of something, e.g. 'cats'.
My word changed in a different way...

Well done for spotting this!

Sometimes the ending might change in a different way, but we are mainly working on 's' and 'es'.

Sometimes the whole word can change (e.g. a 'tooth' and some 'teeth'), and sometimes it doesn't change at all (e.g. a 'sheep' and some 'sheep'). It is good to notice and talk about these too, but they are not the focus of this game.

steps.text: What if I can't add 'er' or 'est'?

Some words can't have 'er' or 'est' added on the end. If you come across any, you could talk about how some words sound funny with those endings, and you just have to say it differently.

Here are some examples:

  • Beautiful:
    • My teddy is beautiful.
    • My teddy is more beautiful.
    • My teddy is the most beautiful.
  • Amazing:
    • My teddy is amazing.
    • My teddy is more amazing.
    • My teddy is the most amazing.
  • Brilliant:
    • My teddy is brilliant.
    • My teddy is more brilliant.
    • My teddy is the most brilliant.

steps.text: For this activity, you will need two toys. Two cuddly teddies will work really well!

How to play:

  1. Think together of some words that describe your teddies.
  2. Player 1 chooses a word and uses it in a sentence.
    E.g. 'My teddy is cuddly.'
  3. Player 2 adds er to the end of the word and uses it about their teddy.
    E.g. 'My teddy is cuddlier than your teddy.'
  4. Player 1 adds est to the end of the word and uses it to show their teddy is the best.
    E.g. 'My teddy is the cuddliest in the whole world.'
  5. Switch who goes first and repeat the game with another word.
  6. Keep taking turns to start, and see how many creative ways you can say how amazing your teddy is!

steps.editorState: Note: some of the words you think of won't have 'ed' endings, e.g. 'swam', 'ran', 'flew'. These are called 'irregular verbs'. It's ok to use some of these, but make sure you also include some 'ed' ending words!

steps.text:
What to do:

Sort the 'ed' words into three lists depending on what sound the 'ed' makes ('t', 'id' or 'd'). Talk together about how you are deciding where to put the cards as you sort them!

When we say words which end with 'ed', the ending makes three different sounds:

  • Sometimes the 'ed' sounds like 't' like in 'pushed';
  • Sometimes the 'ed' sounds like 'id' like in 'sorted';
  • Sometimes the 'ed' sounds like 'd' like in 'called'.


This can make spelling really tricky, but if we think about the different sounds, it can help remember to use 'ed' for all the different sounds.

You will need:

'ed' word cards - use the cards sent home from school or download below (these are the same words as in Activity 1):

No cards?
You could cut out cards from scrap paper or a cereal box and write the punctuation marks on. Or use these:
Pile up the punctuation cards face down, then play these games.

You will need:

Some flour on a tray. Flour works really well because of its fine texture, but you could also try sugar, salt or sand. If you don't have a tray, a large plate would also work.

Warmup:

Take it in turns to write a punctuation mark in the flour. Choose one of these:
  • Full stop .
  • Question mark ?
  • Exclamation mark !
The other person says which punctuation mark you have drawn.

Main activity:

Take it in turns to write a punctuation mark in the flour. The other person says a sentence which ends with the punctuation mark you have drawn.

Read the book aloud to your child. Run your finger under the words as you read so they can see where you are in the writing.

When you get to a punctuation mark, your child should do the Kung Fu action and say the name of the punctuation mark.
How much should we do?

Aim for between five and ten sentences, depending on how much punctuation there is.

If it is tricky to start with, you could try the same sentence more than once instead of doing lots of sentences.

Don't worry about any extra punctuation marks your child has not learned about yet (e.g. commas or apostrophes).

steps.text:
You will need:

A book. It can be a book your child is reading or one you are reading to them.
Kung fu actions

Capital Letter

Touch fingertips together and make a capital A shape above your head.

Full Stop

Punch forward with your fist.

Exclamation mark

Cut a line straight down with a flat hand, then punch with a fist for the dot at the bottom.

Question mark

Cut a curved line down in the shape of a question mark with a flat hand, then punch with a fist for the dot at the bottom.

Before you start:

Go through each punctuation mark and make sure your child recognises them all. You will be looking for full stops, exclamation marks, question marks and capital letters.

You also need to think of a kung fu action for each punctuation mark. Your child might have done this activity before in school. If they already know some actions, use those! Or click the button to see our suggestions:

The activity:

Read the story aloud to your child, running your finger under the words as you read. When you get to a full stop, your child should stamp their foot (or clap their hands).

If they want to read, they can have a go reading aloud too, as long as they keep stamping (or clapping) for the full stops!
For this activity, you will need a story book. It can be a book your child is reading or a book you are reading to them!

What to do:

  1. One person says the first sentence of a story.
  2. When they get to the end of the sentence, they stamp their foot and say, "Full stop."
  3. The other person says the next sentence in the story.
  4. When they get to the end of the sentence, they stamp their foot and say, "Full stop."
  5. Keep taking it in turns to say the next sentence until you get to the end of the story!


What story should we tell?

It can be a story you know, an invented story or a mix of the two!
In this activity, you will work together to tell a story one sentence at a time!
This is just like the classic game of I Spy, but here we use the first phoneme (sound) in the word rather than the letter name!
This can be a really good game to play on journeys! Maybe you could play again on your way to school!

How to play:

  1. Choose who is starting first.
    If you have never played before, the adult should go first.
  2. The first person chooses something they can see.
    Don't tell the other person what it is!
  3. The first person says I spy with my little eye something beginning with "ch".
    Remember to say the phoneme (sound) at the beginning of the word you have chosen.
  4. The other person guesses what it could be.
    Guess things they can see which begins with that sound, e.g. chair, chips or chocolate.
  5. When they have guessed what it is, swap over!
    Take it in turns to pick different things.

Include some sentences that are not questions. Think carefully about the punctuation you need at the end!

  • If it's a question, do a question mark, e.g. 'Where did it go today?' 
  • If it's not a question, do a full stop, e.g. 'This is my shoe.'

How to play:

  1. Ask a question about the object. At the end of the question, use your finger to write a question mark on your child's hand.
  2. Now your child needs to ask a question. At the end of the question, they should use their finger to write a question mark on their own hand. 
  3. Take it in turns to keep asking questions and writing question marks.

Child's hand drawing question marks in flour on a red tray.

How to play:

Take it in turns to say a sentence:
  • If it is a question, the other person writes a question mark in the flour.
  • If it isn't a question, the other person writes a full stop in the flour.

You get one point for each piece of punctuation you write correctly!

You will need:

  • A tray (a large plate would also work);
  • Flour (or sugar, salt or sand).

Warmup:

Look through a book you are reading and see if you can find any exclamation marks. How many can you find?

Discuss:

Ask your child what exclamation marks are for. They should think about exclamation marks in any writing, not just this book. Here are some things exclamation marks are for:
  • When something is surprising;
  • When something is angry;
  • When something is loud;
  • When something is forceful;
  • When something is amazing;
  • Most importantly, they are used in writing to help make the meaning really clear.


Activity:

Choose one sentence which ends with an exclamation mark.
  • How should you read the sentences with an exclamation mark at the end?
  • Read the sentence aloud. Can we hear the exclamation mark in your voice?
  • Practise reading the sentence several times, so it sounds really smooth and fluent, and we can hear what the exclamation mark is doing.
  • If you need to, the adult could read the sentence with the exclamation mark for the child to copy.
  • Try reading some more sentences with exclamation marks, thinking about what the exclamation mark is telling you to do.
How to Make Invisible Ink

You will Need:

  • Lemon juice
  • Water
  • A small pot
  • Something to write with (a cotton bud works really well, or you could use a brush)
  • Paper
Child dipping a cotton bud into a small pot of lemon juice, ready to use it for writing on her paper.

How to Make the Ink:

Make your invisible ink by putting lemon juice and a little water into your pot. If you don't use water, the writing will show up on the paper, but don't use too much! It still needs to be lemony!

How to Reveal Your Message:

When you have written your words and sentences, you will need to leave your paper to dry. When it is dry, your messages should be invisible! Now you are ready to make your messages reappear!

To make the message reappear, you will need to make your paper really hot. This is a job for a grownup! You can use a hot oven, grill or iron (but make sure the iron is not on a steam setting). Watch the paper really carefully while it is heating (to make sure it doesn't catch fire) and take it out from the oven as soon as the message appears. Let the paper cool down and then read your message!

The Aim of the Activity:

Write messages using invisible ink. When your invisible message appears, it will be really surprising, so you are going to write some sentences which use exclamation marks at the end!

Warmup:

Write some words which could be followed by an exclamation mark, e.g.:
  • Bang!
  • Ouch!
  • Wow!
  • Boo!


Activity:

Write some sentences which could end with an exclamation mark, e.g.:
  • Oh grandma, what big eyes you have!
  • What a disaster it was!
  • The glass crashed to the ground!
  • How amazing this holiday has been!

The Activity:

Use the timer to challenge yourself to complete different fine motor activities in 30 seconds. Repeat the activities to see if you can beat your first time!
Playdough recipe

steps.editorState: This no-cook recipe should take you about four minutes to make and keep for around six months! Of course, you could use another recipe or play dough you have bought from a shop instead.

Ingredients:

  • 1 cup plain flour 
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil (baby oil and coconut oil work too) 
  • 1/4 cup salt 
  • 1 tablespoon cream of tartar 
  • 0.5-0.75 cups boiling water (adding in increments until it feels just right) 
  • food colouring (optional) 
  • few drops glycerine (the secret ingredient for extra stretch and shine) (optional) 
  • a sealable bag or box to keep the play dough in when you have finished playing

steps.text: Boiling water safety

steps.editorState:
Method:

  1. Mix the flour, salt, cream of tartar and oil in a mixing bowl. 
  2. Add the foodcolouring (if you are using it) to the hot water and then tip some of the water into the dry ingredients. 
  3. Stir continuously until it becomes a sticky, combined dough, adding more water if it is too dry. 
  4. Add the glycerine, if you are using it. 
  5. Allow it to cool down then take it out of the bowl and knead it vigorously for a couple of minutes until all of the stickiness has gone. The kneading is really important because it's what makes the dough lovely and stretchy. 
  6. If it is still a little sticky then add a bit more flour until it is just right! 
  7. Your playdough is ready to use!

steps.text:
You will Need:

Playdough - you can use playdough you already have or use this recipe to make your own:
Adding to your playdough

Playdough can be even more fun if you have a toolkit of things you could poke into it to add details to your creation.

Here are some ideas of things you could have in your toolkit (choose two or three at a time):
  • Pasta shapes
  • Candles
  • Pebbles
  • Sticks
  • Beads
  • Googly eyes
  • Drinking straws
  • Lolly sticks
  • Buttons

The Activity:

Use your playdough to make an animal or an alien!

Playdough is really good for building the small muscles in your fingers, thumb and hand. Encourage your child to do lots of squashing, squeezing and rolling to really work their muscles!

You can make anything you like! To make it even more fun, why not add something to the playdough?

Have a chat!

Talk to your child about their creation. You could ask questions such as:

  • What does the playdough feel like?
  • Tell me about what you have made
  • What is your animal or alien called?
This game is a really good way to practise one of the phonemes (sounds) your child is working on. In the example, we use sh, but you can use any phoneme you like!

Warmup:

In the instructions, we use the sound sh, but you can choose any sound your child is working on!
  1. Introduce the magic sound sh.
  2. Explain that every time your child hears you say the magic sound, they clap their hands.
  3. Say the sound sh.
  4. Your child should clap!
  5. Say the sound again a few times. Leave gaps between when you say the sound, changing the length of the gap.


Challenge 1:

Say other sounds before you say sh.
For example, 'b, c, v, th, ff, sh'.

Challenge 2:

Ask them to clap when they hear a word that starts with the sound.
You could choose a category, like animals, e.g 'cat, elephant, chimp, shark.'

steps.editorState:
Challenge 3:

Ask them to clap when they hear a word that contains the sound. 

For example, 'goat, donkey fish.'

You will need:

How to play:

  1. Pile up the word cards face down on the table.
  2. Turn over the top card.
  3. Read the word aloud.
  4. Turn the card over so you can't see the word.
  5. Write the word on the paper.
  6. Flip the card back over and check your spelling.
  7. If you made a mistake, copy the correct spelling of the word next to your mistake.
  8. Repeat with the next word in the pile.
  9. There are lots of words, and it can get tiring, so maybe just do five or six words each time you do this activity.


What are the jars for?

You can just use a jar for storing your words, but the two jars are also a really good way of keeping track of which words you can spell and which words need a bit more practice.
  • One jar is the practice jar and the other is a jar for words which you can spell.
  • Keep all the words in the practice jar.
  • If you have spelled a word correctly on three separate occasions, move it into the other jar.
  • Over time, all the words should move from the practice jar into the jar for words you can spell!

Choose words without too many sounds - start with three. Words with more sounds are harder to blend together!
This is just like the classic game of Simon Says, but in this version, Simon breaks one of the words down into its separate sounds, e.g. "r-u-n" instead of "run".

How to play:

  1. Choose who is going to be Simon.
    Simon is in charge of giving the instructions.
  2. Simon gives the instruction, e.g. Simon says j-u-m-p.
    Don't forget to break one of the words down into phonemes (sounds).
  3. The other person follows the instruction.
    Keep going until Simon tells you to stop!
  4. Simon can try to trick the other person .
    If Simon gives the instruction without saying "Simon says", then the other person should not follow the instruction.
  5. Keep going until Simon manages to trick the other person.
    Keep swapping so both people get a chance to give and follow the instructions.

Before you start:

Choose a poem to learn.

You might have your own book of poetry, or you could visit the library and find out what poetry books they have. You could also find a poem online - one of our favourite poems to learn is 'Now We Are Six' by A.A. Milne!

Tip: A shorter poem can be easier for your first try!

The activity:

  1. Read through the poem together and talk about what it means.
    If you really understand what the poem is about, it makes it easier to remember the words.
  2. Look for any patterns in the poem that might make it easier to remember.
    Does it have any repeated words? Does it rhyme?
  3. Read the first line and then say it again without looking.
    Sometimes adding actions can really help you remember the words.
  4. Once you can remember the first line, try the first two lines together.
    Building up sections of the poem together helps remember them in the right order.
  5. Once you can remember the whole poem, practise it several times.
    It should get stuck in your head!
  6. When you know it really well, try performing your poem!
    You could perform it to someone in your family, a friend or even make a video!

You might have one of these books at home, but they should also be easy to find in your local library:

  • 'Each Peach Pear Plum' by Janet and Allan Ahlberg
Front covers of books listed

We like these books for performing because they are stories that are written like poems. Other books by the same authors are also worth looking at!

You can also find videos online of these stories being performed, which can be fun to watch!
Parent and child Mathscot monkeys reading together

Practising and performing a story can be really fun - when you're still working on phonics, reading a story can be hard work, but if you look at it lots of times together and you start to learn the words, suddenly you can 'read' a story by yourself!

If the story is new to your child:
  1. Read the story aloud to your child.
  2. Re-read the story several times - can they start to finish the sentence, e.g. if you leave the rhyming word off the end?
  3. Re-read the story again - can they do some more of the words?


If the story is already familiar to your child:
  1. Read the story aloud to your child - can they finish any of the sentences, e.g. if you leave the rhyming word off the end?
  2. Read the story again - see how many of the words they already know and practise saying them together.
  3. See how much of the story your child can tell by themself - they can use the pictures in the book to help, and you can read any of the words they're not sure about!


Some more things to think about:

  • Speak loudly and clearly (but without shouting);
  • Think about how you could use your body in the performance - you could do actions, or even act out what is happening;
  • Think about how to use the volume of your voice - some parts could be louder or softer;
  • Think about how to use the tone of your voice - you could change how you talk to show how it is exciting, scary or funny.
  • You can do the performance together - it doesn't just need to be your child performing on their own!

Place the dominoes face up on the table and ask your child to pick out one with the same number of dots on each side.

Ask your child to count how many dots there are on each side. Then, ask them how many dots there are altogether.

Explain to your child that if there are three dots on each side, and six dots overall, then that means six is double three.

Repeat the activity to practise doubles.

For this activity you need two teddies and around 10 pennies.

Ask your child to give half of the pennies to each teddy. Ask them to count how many pennies each teddy has, then how many pennies there are overall.

Talk to your child about doubling and halving. For example, if there are four pennies overall, and each teddy has two pennies, then that means four is double two, and two is half of four.

Repeat the activity, changing the number of pennies there are overall each time.

For this activity you will need a mirror.

Ask you child to hold up a number of fingers and count them together.

Then, ask them to count how many fingers there are in the mirror (you could point to each of their fingers in turn as they count them).

Finally, ask them to count how many fingers there are in total (their 'real' ones plus those in the mirror).

E.g. If there are 3 on their hand, and 3 in the mirror, then there are 6 overall. That means 6 is double 3.
Repeat the activity with different numbers and practise talking about doubling and halving with your child.

  6. Which is the funniest sentence?
Tips for Parents

Sometimes children confuse a sentence with a line of writing. Here are some things that might help:
  • You can remind them that a sentence is a whole idea that starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop (or a question mark or exclamation mark).
  • You can say that sometimes the writer has an idea that is too long to fit on one line, so the sentence takes up more room and goes onto the next line.
  • If your child spots a line of writing instead of a sentence, read the line aloud and talk about whether it makes sense – sometimes reading aloud makes it clear that something is missing because the rest of the sentence is on the next line.

For this activity, you will need paper and something to write with.

The Activity

  1. Think about the different ways you can show how you are feeling, e.g. you might laugh or cry. How many ways can you think of?
  2. Choose one of those ways of showing feelings and think about what might make you feel like that, e.g. ‘laugh’ – my brother tickled my toes.
  3. Write down a sentence for that feeling using this structure: ‘I would____ if____.’ E.g. I would laugh if my brother tickled my toes.
  4. See if you can write down five sentences for five different feelings.

How to play:

  1. Player 1 thinks of a famous person.
    The person can be real or fictional, alive or dead. They should be someone both players have heard of.
  2. Player 1 then tells Player 2 the first letter of their person’s name.
    Usually this will be the first letter of their surname, e.g. “R” for Christiano Ronaldo or “O” for Michelle Obama, though sometimes a person is known by their first name alone, so you would need to use that letter instead, e.g. “L” for Lorde or “A” for Adele.
  3. Player 2 must think of a person it could be and ask a question that could give that person as the answer.
    E.g. if the letter was “D”, then the person could be Roald Dahl, so they could ask, “Are you a children’s author?”
  4. Player 1 must then answer the question.
    There are four possible things that could happen:
    1. Player 1 answers, “No, I am not Roald Dahl.” Player 2 will then need to ask more questions.
    2. Player 1 answers, “No, I am not Julia Donaldson.” This might mean their person is Roald Dahl but further questions would be needed to check.
    3. Player 1 can’t think of an alternative as in example ii, and so is forced to answer, “Yes, I am Roald Dahl” and Player 2 wins.
    4. Player 1 can’t think of a children’s author beginning “D” and so has to say, “No, and I don’t know who you are thinking of.” If this happens, Player 2 must say who they were thinking of, and then they are allowed to ask one yes/no question about the person to help narrow down who it could be.
  5. Player 2 keeps asking questions until they have found out who it is.
    If it starts becoming too difficult, Player 1 can say who their person was and they win the game.
Why is the game called Botticelli?
Sandro Botticelli is a famous artist, who lived in Italy from 1445 to 1510. The name comes from the idea that the person you choose should be at least as famous as Botticelli.

For this activity, you will need two pieces of paper and two things to write with (ideally two different colours).

What to do:

  1. Line 1
    Write the beginning of a sentence starting with ‘If’. Don’t put a full stop – the other person is going to finish your sentence. Instead, finish with a comma.
    e.g. 'If the world was made of custard',
    Fold the paper over to hide your writing.
  2. Line 2
    Swap paper (don’t look at what the other person wrote).
    Write something to finish off the hidden sentence – write it like this ‘something would/should/will/could __________’e.g.:
    • a hare will dig a hole.
    • cake would be well cooked.
    • Grandma will sneeze.
  3. Line 3
    Keeping the same piece of paper, on a new line, use the words you just wrote to start a new ‘If’ sentence (ending with a comma).
    e.g. you wrote ‘Grandma will sneeze’ so now you write ‘If Grandma sneezes’.
    Fold the paper over to hide your writing.
  4. Line 4
    Swap with the other person and again write something to finish the sentence.
  5. Line 5
    Again, Keeping the same piece of paper, on a new line, use the words you just wrote to start a new ‘If’ sentence.
  6. Lines 6+
    After 3 or 4 sentences, unravel the paper and have a look!

The Game:

Imagine you are both at a party. The Host is welcoming guests and talking to them. But one guest arrives and the Host does not know who they are. This new person is the Mystery Visitor! Choose one person to be the Host and one person to be the Mystery Visitor.

Before you start:

The person being the Mystery Visitor must choose someone to be. Pick a person who is famous or fictional (choose someone you both know about).

How to Play:

  1. The Mystery Visitor leaves the room, then comes back in pretending to be their person. Try to move like the person and talk like the person.
  2. The Host welcomes the Mystery Visitor to the party and asks questions to find out more about them. The Mystery Visitor must answer as their character. For instance:

    Host: Welcome to my party! Would you like a drink?
    Visitor: Yes please. Could I have pink milk please?
    Host: Of course! Here you go!
    Visitor: Thank you! Slurp! Oooh yummy!
    Host: Can I get you something to eat? How about some of these delicious tomatoes?
    Visitor: Oh no! I will not ever, never eat a tomato!

  3. When the Host thinks they have worked out who the Mystery Visitor is, they can ask “Are you___?” If they have guessed correctly, the game ends. If not, they should ask some more questions!
  4. When you have finished, swap over so the other person can have a go at being the Mystery Visitor.

Examples:
  • I like fish and I like chips but I don't like mushy peas.
  • I like horses and I like elephants but I don’t like spiders.
  • I like running and I like football but I don’t like golf.

The Activity:

You are each going to pretend to be a fictional character and write letters to each other as your characters.

What to do:

  1. Choose a fictional character each. They can be from the same book (or film or TV programme) or different ones.
  2. One person writes a letter from their character to the other.
  3. When the second person receives the letter, they should read it and then write a reply.
  4. Keep writing replies to each other until you have had a few goes!
What Should I Write?

• Think about how your character might write. Try to make your writing sound like them and include things they would know about or do.
  • Think about how to start your letter:
    • Do your characters know each other?
    • Are they friends, enemies or something else?
    • Is this the first time they’ve written to each other, or might they have written in the past?
  • Think about why they might be writing to each other. They could be:
    • Sharing news,
    • Setting up a meeting,
    • Inviting them to something,
    • Complaining about something.
  • Don’t worry about making it too long – three paragraphs is probably a good length, and gives you space to include:
    • An introduction to why you are writing,
    • A middle part with the main points in,
    • A closing part with something that will make them want to reply.
  • Try to give the other person something to reply to. You could:
    • Ask a question,
      • Say something you know they will want to disagree with,
    • Ask for advice about something.

Don’t mind spending a bit more time?

You could do this activity with someone who doesn’t live in your house! You could put your letter in the post, or take a photo an text or email it, or even type it up as an email!

What should I write?


Here are some things you could think about:
Work together to build an expanded noun phrase. You don’t need to write anything down for this game – just say your ideas!

How to Play:

  1. Player 1 chooses a noun, e.g. ‘bicycle’.
  2. Player 2 adds a determiner, e.g. ‘a bicycle’. This is a noun phrase.
  3. Player 1 adds an adjective, e.g. ‘a green bicycle’. This is an expanded noun phrase.
  4. Player 2 adds another adjective, e.g. ‘a big, green bicycle’.
  5. Take it in turns to add adjectives until it gets too silly!
  6. Try again with a different noun.

  • For each letter of the alphabet, work together to write an expanded noun phrase for an animal beginning with that letter.
