steps.text:
The Activity:

Do a presentation about an artwork. You might need to make notes to help you remember what to say, but don't write out the whole speech or you'll just end up reading it out!

What artworks could I use?

  • A drawing you have done yourself (maybe you could make a frame and put it on the wall).
  • A picture you already have on the wall in your house.
  • A picture of a famous artwork in a book or online.
  • A real artwork in a museum or art gallery.

Does my presentation have to be true?

You could do some research so that your presentation contains some factual information, or you could invent your own “facts” (even if it is a real artwork).

What should I say?

  • When the artwork was created
  • Who created it
  • What they used to make it
  • What it represents
  • Any interesting details – things that your audience might not have noticed
  • Some information about the artwork’s history – maybe it was once stolen and then found years later, or maybe it was discovered in an attic…
  • Anything else you like!

Where should I do my presentation?

It is probably best if you have either the real artwork or a picture of it so that the person you are talking to can see what you are talking about. If you have chosen an artwork in a local gallery, it could be fun to go to the gallery and do your presentation next to the real thing!

The Activity:

Do a presentation about an artwork. You might need to make notes to help you remember what to say, but don't write out the whole speech or you'll just end up reading it out!

What artworks could I use?

  • A drawing you have done yourself (maybe you could make a frame and put it on the wall).
  • A picture you already have on the wall in your house.
  • A picture of a famous artwork in a book or online.
  • A real artwork in a museum or art gallery.

Does my presentation have to be true?

You could do some research so that your presentation contains some factual information, or you could invent your own “facts” (even if it is a real artwork).

What should I say?

  • When the artwork was created
  • Who created it
  • What they used to make it
  • What it represents
  • Any interesting details – things that your audience might not have noticed
  • Some information about the artwork’s history – maybe it was once stolen and then found years later, or maybe it was discovered in an attic…
  • Anything else you like!

Where should I do my presentation?

It is probably best if you have either the real artwork or a picture of it so that the person you are talking to can see what you are talking about. If you have chosen an artwork in a local gallery, it could be fun to go to the gallery and do your presentation next to the real thing!

In the game ‘Simon Says’, there are two kinds of instructions:
  • Instructions that begin ‘Simon says’.
  • Instructions that do not begin ‘Simon says’.


The person following the instructions must listen carefully:
  • If the instruction begins ‘Simon says,’ they should follow it.
  • If the instruction does not begin ‘Simon says,’ they should not follow it.
Simon Says Example Game

Simon: Simon says jump up and down.
Player 2 jumps up and down.
Simon: Simon says clap hands.
Player 2 claps hands.
Simon: Sing a song.
Player 2 does not sing a song (well done for spotting the trick).
Simon: Simon says whistle.
Player 2 whistles.
Simon: Run round the room backwards.
Player 2 runs round the room backwards.
Simon: You’re out! I didn’t’ say ‘Simon says!’
Players swap over so the other person can have a go at being Simon.

How to Play:

  1. Decide who is being Simon. Simon will give the instructions; Player 2 will follow them.
  2. Simon says an instruction.
  3. Player 2 listens carefully and decides whether to follow it.
  4. Simon keeps giving instructions and Player 2 follows until Simon catches Player 2 out. This happens if Player 2 follows and instruction that did not start ‘Simon says’.
  5. When Player 2 has been caught out, swap over so the other person can have a go at being Simon.

What to do:

  1. Choose your fairy-tale event. There are some ideas here (or you can choose your own):
    • A wolf has been roaming the streets and blowing down pigs’ houses!
    • An enormous beanstalk was suddenly found growing in Jack’s garden!
    • Wedding of the Century – Cinderella and Prince Charming are getting married!
    • Porridge stolen and house wrecked by mysterious golden-haired girl!
  2. On a piece of paper, make a mind-map to sort out your ideas – write your topic in the centre and your ideas around it.
  3. Decide on your opening sentence – it needs to be something that grabs the attention of the people watching/listening and tells them what the story will be about, for instance, “This morning, passers-by discovered an enormous beanstalk growing in Jack’s front garden.”
  4. Think about what order to include the ideas from your mind map.
  5. Decide on your closing sentence – it needs to be something that reminds people what the news story was about and why it was important.
  6. Make notes to help you remember what to say – you don’t necessarily need to write out all the words, just enough so you don’t forget anything!
  7. Present your news report – you could use someone in your house as your audience, video call someone you know, or film it!

Example game:

Stripy, small, hard, shiny, round, cold, solid, new, fragile, useful, smooth, breakable, clean, curved…

How to Play:

  1. Choose an object in your house, e.g. a bowl.
  2. Take it in turns to say a word that describes the object. These words are adjectives.
  3. Count how many adjectives you thought of altogether.
  4. Repeat with another object. Did you think of more or fewer adjectives?

1. Describe what the animal smells like.
    You can use as many words as you like (but don’t say what the animal is). Don’t worry if you don’t know what it really smells like – imagine how it might smell.
    5 points
  2. Describe what the animal feels like to touch.
    You can use as many words as you like (but remember not to say what it looks like).
    4 points
  3. Describe how the animal moves.
    You can use as many words as you like (but don’t say what the animal is).
    3 points
  4. Describe how the animal sounds.
    You can use as many words as you like (but try not to make the actual noise).
    2 points
  5. Describe where the animal lives.
    You can use as many words as you like (but don’t say the place name, just say what the place is like).
    1 point
    If they don’t guess correctly, you can tell them the answer!


When the other player has guessed what your animal is, swap over so they can have a go at describing. Repeat a few times and see if you can improve your scores!

Still not sure what to do?

Have a look at this example game:
Describing an Animal Example

1. Describe what the animal smells like.
It smells damp and fishy, a bit like seaweed that’s washed up on the beach, but maybe a bit more meaty.

2. Describe what the animal feels like to touch.
If you stroke it in one direction, it feels cold and smooth and damp. But in the other direction, it feels rough like sandpaper.

3. Describe how the animal moves.
It glides smoothly, its whole body snaking from side to side. Sometimes it moves slowly and sometimes it suddenly bursts forward.

4. Describe how the animal sounds.
This creature moves as silently as a ghost. You wouldn’t want to hear the crunch of its powerful jaws.

5. Describe where the animal lives.
Sunshine ripples down into the cool, blue, salty water. Sometimes it is smooth and calm, and other times it is stormy and rough.
In this example, we haven’t shown any of the guesses because we wanted to show the whole description. If the other player guesses after the first description, it stops there!

How to Play:

Think of an animal and describe it to the other person using the five steps below. For each step, the other person is allowed to make one guess. The sooner they guess, the more points you get!

steps.text:
For this activity, you will need:

A paragraph to read. You can choose something from a book you have, or you can use this extract from Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland.
We chose this piece because one character is talking all the way through, which means you can pretend you are an actor in a play (if you like).

What to do:

  1. Read your paragraph out loud. Check it all makes sense to you and think about what is happening.
  2. How can you use your voice to show how the character is feeling? Think about the way you would say the words if it was happening to you in real life!
  3. If your paragraph has speech and narration, think about how to change your voice to show the difference between the character(s) speaking and the narrator.
  4. Read it again two or three times, thinking carefully about how you use your voice to make the meaning clear.
  5. Now it’s getting more familiar, try adding in some facial expressions that would help show how the character is feeling or what they are thinking.
  6. Once you’ve read it a few more times, you might find you don’t need to look at the writing the whole time you are speaking. If you get to this point, you might be able to add in some movements for your character, as if you were an actor on the stage!
  7. Find an audience – it could be someone in your house, on a video call, or you could film yourself – and perform it for them!

You Will Need:

A reading book. In can be a book from school, from the library or from home. Before you start, check the book has some speech marks in it!

The Activity:

  1. Find some inverted commas in your book.
  2. Which words are being spoken?
  3. Who is talking?
  4. Does the writing tell you how they are talking?
  5. Have a go at reading the sentence (including the part outside the speech marks which tells you who said it). Try using a different voice when the character is speaking!
  6. Have another go with some different sentences in the book! Can you use different voices for different characters?
Speech marks are sometimes called inverted commas, and they are used in writing to show when someone is speaking. Here is an example:
In this example, you can see how the 66-shaped inverted commas show where the speech begins, and the 99-shaped inverted commas show where the speech ends.
Top Tips for Writing Speech Marks

• At the start, the speech marks look a bit like 66 (without a hole in the middle).
  • At the end, the speech marks look a bit like 99 (without a hole in the middle).
  • The dot should be the size of a full stop.
  • The shape of each speech mark should be like a comma, with a little flick (the first two are like upside-down commas).
  • The speech marks should be level with the top of your capital letters.
  • Try not to make them too big – they are small like commas and full stops, not big like letters!

details.name: Top Tips for Writing Speech Marks

You Will Need:

Something you can use to write really big letters. Here are some ideas:
  • Chalks on the ground outdoors

What to Do:

  1. Think of lots of different animal noises, e.g. Moo, Baa, Woof etc.
  2. Write the animal noise words in big letters around your space. Start each one with a capital letter and end with an exclamation mark.
  3. Once you have written the noises, take it in turns to add speech marks to each noise.

Part 1: Draw Your Picture

  1. Draw a picture of two characters from a story.
  2. Then give each one a speech bubble and write inside what they are saying to each other.

Part 2: Write Two Sentences

Write two sentences underneath using inverted commas to show what they are saying, in the form "___" said ___. "___" said ___.

Use these steps to help you:
  1. Start by writing the words from your speech bubble.
  2. If you used a full stop at the end of the sentence in your speech bubble, change it to a comma in this sentence. If you used an exclamation or question mark, it can stay the same.
  3. Then add the inverted commas.
  4. Then add 'said___.'

Example:

These sentences use ‘then’ in three different places.
  • Then the tiger opened its mouth.
  • The tiger then opened its mouth.
  • The tiger opened its mouth then.


Challenge:

Choose your favourite sentence and write it down.
  1. How many different places can you put the same adverb in the sentence? Write down these sentences.
  2. Do all your sentences mean exactly the same thing?
  3. Which sentence do you like best and why?

Activity:

  1. Choose one of the adverbs from the list below.
  2. Say a sentence using the adverb.
  3. Think about where in the sentence you put the adverb.
  4. Try using the same adverb in a different place in the sentence.
  5. Repeat with some of the other adverbs.
Example game

steps.editorState:
Scene 1 (first syllable):

Player 1 acts out a battle between her and her mortal enemy. She says things like, “Aha, I see my foe behind that rock!” and “You will not get away from me!”

Player 2 thinks about what one syllable words were included, e.g. ‘see’, ‘my’, ‘foe’, ‘you’ etc.

Guessing the word:

Which of the three syllable words in the last scene had syllables which featured in earlier scenes?

  • “Rocketed” is a possibility – “rock” was in the first scene – but he can’t remember hearing “ted” in the third scene.
  • Maybe “photograph?” Oh yes, there was a “toe” in the scene at the doctors. And she was fighting a “foe” in the first scene. It must be “photograph”! 

Player 2 guesses “photograph” and Player 1 says he was correct!

The players then swap over, and Player 2 chooses a word to act out.

Scene 4 (whole word):

Player 1 thinks of some three syllable words to include in this scene. She must include “photograph” as this was her chosen word but having some more will make it harder to guess. She chooses “awarding”, “designer” and “rocketed”. She pretends to be a reporter at an awards ceremony, interviewing the actor Melanie Jackman about her new film. She says things like, “Melanie, how has it been since you rocketed to fame when this film came out?” and “Could you possibly pose for a photograph?”

Player 2 listens out for all the three syllable words.

Scene 2 (second syllable):

Player 1 acts out a trip to the doctor. She is the doctor and asks her teddy (the patient) what is wrong with them. She says things like, “Is there a problem with your eye?” and “Let me have a look at your toe.”

Player 2 again thinks about what one syllable words were included.

Scene 3 (third syllable):

Player 1 pretends to be a nutritionist sharing some information about popular foods. She is presenting her ideas to an audience. She says things like, “Most kids like to eat lots of sweets!” and “If you look at this graph, you will see that in the UK, jam is getting less popular as a toast topping over time.”

Player 2 again thinks about what one syllable words were included.

Getting ready:

Player 1 chooses the word “photograph” and splits it into three syllables for the first three scenes:

  1. “foe”
  2. “toe” 
  3. “graph”

steps.text: Hints to help Player 2 guess

steps.editorState:
• Listen for any one syllable words included in the first three scenes.
  • Listen for all the three syllable words included in the fourth scene.
  • If you hear a three syllable word in the fourth scene, see if you recognise any of its parts from the earlier scenes!

steps.text: Choosing your word

steps.editorState:
Think about what you could say for each syllable – it’s easier if the syllables sound like real words:

  • “Tricycle” can be broken down into “try”, “sick” and “all” (which are all real words)
  • “Banana” will be harder because “ban” is a real word but “arr” and “nah” are just sounds (though you could still do this, you just need to be more creative – maybe have a Pirate in the second scene who says “arr” and someone who disagrees in the third scene by saying “nah”).

Suggestions of three syllable words:

Amazing: a, may, zing

Microwave: my, crow, wave

Recycle: re, sigh, call

Terrible: tear, rib, all

Waterfall: wart, er, fall

steps.text:
Activity:

Write instructions for how to make breakfast (or you could choose another meal).

You must:
  • Think about what to do before you start;
  • Include at least five steps;
  • Use a number to start each step;
  • Use an adverb at the start of each step to help make them easier to follow. You can choose from the list below or come up with your own;
  • Try not to use the same adverb more than once;
  • If you are feeling fancy, see if you can use a comma after the adverb, e.g. ‘First, put a plate on the table.’


Adverbs You Could Use:

first, then, next, slowly, carefully, finally
Example Instructions with Adverbs

How to Make Breakfast

You Will Need:
  • Bowl
  • Spoon
  • Cereal
  • Milk


What to Do:
  1. First, set the table with everything you need.
  2. Next, put cereal in your bowl.
  3. Then, pour milk over your cereal.
  4. After that, eat it up!
  5. Finally, when you have finished eating, clear the table and put the milk back in the fridge.

The Activity:

1. Mina ran excitedly along the beach as the waves crashed lazily on the shore.

  2. The woman stared proudly at the child balancing carefully along the wall.

  3. The witch stared coldly at the kitten miaowing pitifully outside her door.

You Will Need:

  • A piece of paper;
  • Something to write with;
  • A window to look out of.

The Activity:

Look out of the window. Write a list of what you can see, using a/an before each thing.

Remember, ‘a’ comes before words that start with a consonant sound and ‘an’ comes before words that start with a vowel sound. For example, ‘a car’ or ‘an elephant’ (though you’d be lucky to spot an elephant out of your window).

Increase the Challenge:

See if you can spot something for every letter of the alphabet.

Challenge 2:

Sometimes we use ‘a’ or ‘an’ before a short phrase, e.g. ‘a beautiful flower’ or ‘an excellent horse’. With these, it is the first word in the phrase which determines whether you should use ‘a’ or ‘an’.

Say whether these phrases need ‘a’ or ‘an’:

Challenge 1:

Say whether these words need ‘a’ or ‘an’:
In these three examples, it seems like a/an have been used incorrectly. But they are right. Can you figure out why? Saying them aloud might help!

an hour
a unicorn
an x-ray

steps.text: Look at these three things:
The Solution

Although we usually look at the first letter to work out whether to use ‘a’ or ‘an’, it’s actually the first sound in a word which is important.

In these examples, ‘hour’ begins with the vowel sound ‘ow’, ‘unicorn’ begins with the consonant sound ‘y’ and ‘x-ray’ begins with the vowel sound ‘e’.

A cat.
Check Your Work

Many people keep cats as pets. But why could this be? Perhaps it’s because cats are furry, friendly and lots of fun. Cats love to play. They are also very intelligent and sociable, which makes them great pets. They are amazing at jumping and can run really fast. They can also squeeze through small spaces: unlike ours, cats’ collarbones are not fixed to other bones, which means their shoulders can get narrower to fit through gaps.

It is thought that the Romans probably first brought cats to Britain to help control pests such as rats and mice. Nowadays, cats are still used for pest control, but they are also kept simply as pets. There are even some famous pet cats! Taylor Swift’s cat is called Meredith Grey and she is something of a social media star.

Another famous cat is Larry, who lives in the Prime Minister’s house at 10 Downing Street. His official title is Chief Mouser to the Cabinet office. Larry hasn’t always got on with everyone, though he did enjoy a visit from Barrack Obama: Ex-Prime Minister David Cameron said, “Obama gave him a stroke and he was all right with Obama.”

Challenge:

Make some of your own cards to add to the game. Remember, there must only be one mistake on each card.

The Aim of the Game:

Each card has one mistake on it. It might be a spelling mistake, or it might be a punctuation mistake. You need to spot the mistakes and see if you can correct them!

What to Do:

  1. Pile the cards in a stack face down.
  2. Turn over the top card.
  3. When you spot the mistake, say “Bing!”
  4. Tell the other person what mistake you spotted and how you would correct it.
  5. If you’re not sure whether you are right, you can check using the pdf below.
  6. You get one point for spotting the mistake and a bonus point if you accurately correct it.
  7. Keep turning over cards one at a time and see if you can spot the mistakes.
  8. At the end of the game, the person with the most points wins!

Can you tell a whole fairy tale in only three sentences?
Jack and the Beanstalk

This version of Jack and the Beanstalk is written using only three sentences!

Once there was a poor boy called Jack, who swapped his cow for some magic beans. At the top of the beanstalk which grew, Jack found a giant’s castle and a magic hen that laid golden eggs. Jack stole the giant’s hen, but luckily Jack’s mother was ready and cut down the beanstalk as the giant chased him down, so they were able to live happy and rich for ever after.

Warmup:

Choose a job (look at the balloon below if you need ideas) and work together to order the personality words by how important they are for a particular job. At this point, you might decide to write some new personality describing words to add to your collection.

Preparation:

Together, think of ten (or more) words that can be used to describe a person (e.g. clever, boring, excitable, beautiful). Write them on scraps of paper so you can move the words around on the table.

Activity:

  1. Player 1 chooses a job but doesn't tell the other person what it is
  2. Player 1 puts the words for their chosen job in order from most to least important.
  3. Player 2 guesses what the job is from the order of the words.
  4. Once Player 2 has guessed, they should say whether they agree or disagree with Player 1’s order and why.
  5. Swap over and repeat.

Watch a poet performing their poem and talk about what you like about their performance.

Michael Rosen is a good example of a poet who uses their performance to help you enjoy their poems even more. This page of his website has some good poems to choose from. You could pick anything, though ‘Strict’ is particularly fun!

The Activity:

Read the three poems and choose one to perform.

What to do:

  1. Check you can say all the words.
  2. Check you know what it means. If you’re not sure, talk about it together.
  3. Think about the rhythm of the poem – check you can say the lines with the rhythm. You might need to practise a few times to get it sounding right.
  4. Think about how loud you are saying the words – the audience need to hear but you don’t want to do it so loudly they think you are shouting at them.
  5. Think about how to make the poem more interesting to listen to – can you do a different voice for speech? Can you use your voice to help make the meaning clear?
  6. Think about how to make the poem more interesting to watch – if you have a mirror, try saying the poem to yourself in the mirror and look at what your face is doing.
  7. Find someone at home and perform your poem to them. Maybe you could film your performance to send to your teacher!

Here are two ideas to get you started (but you can write any kind of poem you like):

Idea 1

Write a limerick, like the ones you read in Activity 2.
  1. Have another read of the examples in Activity 2 to get the rhythm in your head.
  2. Think about the rhyming word at the end of the first line to get you started. That should be your first line sorted, starting with “There was a” and ending with your rhyming word.
  3. Try saying the words out loud until you have a poem that you’re happy with, then write it down so you don’t forget it!


Idea 2

Talk with your pen. This sounds like a funny idea, but it’s the kind of thing Michael Rosen does in lots of his poems, including ‘Strict’ in Activity 1. Talking with your pen is where you just write down some thoughts or ideas, maybe about something you’ve seen or heard.
  1. Imagine that you’re telling someone about it, but instead of saying the words, write them down.
  2. Michael Rosen turns these ideas into poems partly through the way he repeats lines. See if you can include some repetition to turn your thoughts into a poem.
Read this question ↑ and then talk about it together.

This conversation is called a discussion. In a discussion, you should:

  • Make sure both people have a chance to talk.
  • Listen to what the other person has to say.
  • Be polite to each other, including valuing what the other person says (though this doesn’t mean you always have to agree).
  • Respond to what the other person says, maybe saying, “I agree because…” or “I disagree because…”
  • Build on what the other person says.
  • Keep on topic – don’t start talking about something else!
  • Explain your opinions with reasons.
  • Speak loudly enough for the other person to hear you but not so loudly they don’t want to listen.

Setting up:

  1. Choose sixteen children’s books that could potentially win the competition ‘Best Children’s Book of All Time’. Remember, it can include any children’s books you like, including picture books and novels. It is fun to have a mix! Make sure you both know all the books!
  2. Write the book titles on separate scraps of paper. Put them into a bowl or hat.
  3. Pull out two titles at a time and write the pairs onto the World Cup sheet in the ‘Last Sixteen’ spaces.
  4. Keep going until all the ‘Last Sixteen’ spaces are filled.

How to play:

  1. For each pair of books, each player must choose a book to support.
  2. Think of reasons why your book is better than the other.
  3. Debate which book should go through to the next round, sharing your reasons. You need to argue for your book, but eventually you will need to come to an agreement.
  4. Write the winning book in the ‘Quarter Finals’ space.
  5. Repeat with the other books in the ‘Last Sixteen’ round so you end up with eight quarter-finalists.
  6. Once you have all your quarter-finalists, repeat the process with your new pairs to see which four books go through to the Semi Finals.
  7. Repeat your debate with your semi-finalists to fund your two finalists.
  8. Debate your two finalists to find out who wins the award ‘Best Children’s Book of All Time’!

You will need:

  • A printout of the World Cup sheet (or use it to draw your own)
  • Something to write with
  • Sixteen scraps of paper

In this activity, you will be giving someone a really clear explanation to help them do something. You need to choose an everyday task for the activity that you don’t mind doing twice!
In this activity, you will be giving someone a really clear explanation to help them do something. You need to choose an everyday task for the activity that you don’t mind doing twice!

What to do:

  1. Choose an everyday task, e.g. brushing your teeth.
  2. Explain to the other person how to do it.
  3. While you are explaining, they should do the task. They should your instructions carefully.
  4. Watch closely what they are doing – are your instructions easy to follow?
  5. Now imagine the other person is an alien who has never brushed their teeth before, or even seen a toothbrush or sink.
  6. Explain how to do the task again, but this time make sure the instructions are something that an alien would be able to follow.
  7. While you are explaining, they should pretend to be an alien and do the task. They might get things wrong if your explanation is not clear!


Tip for Grownups:

When you are pretending to be the alien, you can pretend to misunderstand any instructions which are unclear. Your child might have to explain in a different way to help you understand!

What to Do:

  1. Choose a topic you do not agree on (or you can pretend you don’t agree). See below for some ideas.
  2. Stand opposite each other at different sides of the room (you should be fairly far apart).
  3. Player 1 says her side of the argument.
  4. Player 2 says his side of the argument.
  5. Player 1 thinks of something she could do to help settle the differences between them.
  6. Player 2 thinks about this offer and says why (or why not) he is prepared to accept this proposal.
  7. If Player 2 accepts the proposal, Player 1 takes a step forward. If Player 2 does not accept the proposal, Player 1 stays still.
  8. Now Player 2 thinks of something she could do to help settle the differences between them and Player 1 says why (or why not) she is prepared to accept it. If Player 1 accepts the offer, Player 2 takes a step forward.
  9. Keep repeating this, taking turns to suggest something, until you are close enough to shake hands. When this happens, you have found a workable compromise and can shake hands on your settlement.

  1. Tell your child that you've found this interesting thing or picture and you want to chat about it.
  2. Begin by saying "I notice…" and completing the sentence with something you notice, e.g. if it is a sieve, "I notice it has lots of little holes in it."

  4. You could do a couple of things you notice each.
  5. Repeat with "I think" and "I wonder".

The Activity:

Both people should do the activity.
  1. Decide which book you think is the best book ever. You can talk together or think on your own.
  2. Think of some reasons that it is the best book ever. If you want, you could make some notes to help you remember your ideas. Here are some things you could think about:
    • What did you enjoy about it?
    • Do other people like it?
    • Is there anything you can learn from it?
    • What is important about this book?
    • Are there any other books like it?
    • Why is it better than the other books you talked about in the warmup?
  3. Explain to the other person why your book is the best book ever.
  4. Listen to what the other person has to say.
  5. Talk together about why you agreed or disagreed on the best book. Is it possible for there to be only one best book?

  2. Think of some reasons that it is the best book ever. If you want, you could make some notes to help you remember your ideas. Here are some things you could think about:
    • What did you enjoy about it?
    • Do other people like it?
    • Is there anything you can learn from it?
    • What is important about this book?
    • Are there any other books like it?
    • Why is it better than the other books you talked about in the warmup?
  3. Explain to the other person why your book is the best book ever.
  4. Listen to what the other person has to say.
  5. Talk together about why you agreed or disagreed on the best book. Is it possible for there to be only one best book?

One-minute first ideas:

  • Think about the type of presentation you want to do – are you going to do “A History of Me” from when you were born to now, or are you going to do something about how you are now?
  • Think about the important things to include – some of it might be facts, like your age or what foods you like, and some of it might be trickier to explain, like your feelings about particular things or what your personality is like. You can decide what you want to share, and what you think is important.


Two-minute planning:

  • Make notes of what you are going to say. Don’t write every single word, because presentations sound better when you speak rather than read out your notes.


Two-minute practising:

  • Practise saying your words a few times. This will help you check if it feels about the right length, and also make sure your notes help you remember everything you want to say.


One-minute presentation:

  • Decide who is going to go first. The other person will get to speak afterwards!
  • Make sure you speak clearly so your audience can hear what you are saying.
  • Use your notes to help you remember what to say!
  • When you’ve finished, spend a minute listening to the other person’s presentation.

In this activity, you are both rival designers for a book publisher. You will both be designing a cover for a new book, competing to see whose title and blurb will be chosen for the final book!

Before you Start:

Work together to decide which book you are designing the cover for. Here are some ideas:
  • A book you have both read
  • A TV series you have both watched
  • A film you have both seen
  • Something else!

Choose something you both know pretty well so you can imagine what the book might say inside. But don’t choose something with a cover you remember, otherwise you might accidentally copy the original!

What to Do:

The winner will be the person who comes up with the best title and blurb for the book. You can design the pictures and layout if you want, but don’t forget that the competition is all about the words!

  1. On a piece of paper, write a new title for the book.
    • Don’t use the original title.
    • Think carefully what the book is about and make sure the title fits.
    • Keep it quite short so it is easy to see.
    • Try and make it interesting or exciting so that it makes someone want to read the book.
  2. Below the title, write a new blurb for the book.
    • A blurb is usually between 100 and 200 words long. Try to stick to this!
    • Remember that a blurb is trying to tempt someone to read the book – it should make the person want to read more.
    • The blurb needs to show what is in the book without giving too much away – it would be rubbish if the blurb told you the ending!
    • Make sure the blurb matches the tone of the book – if the book is exciting, it needs to be exciting, but if the book is a serious non-fiction text, you might need something more serious.
  3. When you have finished, read through and check you work. You might decide to make some changes and improvements.
  4. When you have both finished, read each other’s title and blurb. Talk together about what you like and compare what you have both written. Which will win? Why?

Preparation:

Take a walk outside, it could be in a garden, park or just down the street. Try to find three interesting things to bring back with you.

The Activity:

Imagine you are a museum creator – this is a person who looks after the objects in a museum, chooses how they are displayed, and helps to explain what they are and why they are important. The three objects you found on your walk are going to be the objects in your museum.

  1. Display your objects. You could set them out on a table with labels saying what they are (or you might have another idea).
  2. Imagine you are going to take someone on a tour of your museum. What will you tell them about each object? You could make notes to help you remember.
  3. Show someone your objects. Explain who you are and welcome them to the museum, then take them to see the three objects and tell your guest all about them.


What if an object isn’t very interesting and I don’t know what to say?

Perhaps you found a leaf on your walk. What could you say?

  • You could decide to be scientific and talk about the kind of plant it is from and why leaves are important to plants.
  • You could invent a story that explains why the leaf is important – maybe the King of Persia plucked this leaf from the magical Oolibub tree and it flew with him across the earth and carried him to meet the famous talking snake of Durble.
  • You could think about it as a work of art – perhaps it represents the changing seasons and the particular colours of the leaf are important because of the way they show the warmth of the sun on an autumn day.

A haiku is a short poem originally from Japan. It has a very strict structure with three lines. The first line has five syllables, the second line has seven syllables and the third line has five syllables.
Here is an example:

The Activity:

Write your own Haiku story. Both of you should write one, and then guess which story the other person’s Haiku is about!
  1. Choose a story. It’s easier if it’s a story that lots of people know. Fairy tales work well!
  2. Think about the important parts of the story – what must you include to help them guess? Try not to include the story title though – that would be too easy!
  3. Try saying your ideas and count the syllables on your fingers as you say them. When you have something that works, write it down. It might not end up in your final poem, but you don’t want to forget it.
  4. Try out lots of ideas until you are happy with your poem as a whole. Then write down the finished haiku.
  5. When you have both finished, read your haikus aloud and try to guess which stories they come from!

carouselData.textEditorState: Once upon a time, there was an enormous ogre who lived in a cavern deep in the darkest forest in the kingdom.
Grelda had been walking in the woods for three days before she found the little cottage with the green door.
Busby leapt nimbly out of the window, climbed down the wall, and scampered across the yard to freedom.
What an amazing day it had been! Well, amazing until grandma had set the boat on fire.
If you’ve ever been given three wishes, you’ll know exactly what Micky asked for when the genie appeared from the lamp.
There was a strange silence in the city, only an old tin can rattling across the pavement, and Lenny wondered whether the hot summer sun had made everyone sleepy.
Ruby drew her sword and stepped out though the castle gates.
The landing pod lowered its wheels and the thrusters slowly pushed it towards the dusty surface of the planet below.

Tell your Story:

How to Play:

  1. Player 1 writes the first line of a story. The last bit of the line goes on the line/space below as a “hook” for the next person to finish. Make sure it is an unfinished sentence so that the first thing they need to do is finish the sentence.
  2. Player 2 finishes the sentence and starts a new one, again leaving a “hook” on the next line.
  3. Keep swapping over until you get to the end.
  4. Unfold the paper and see what story you have written!


How to Make it Really Good:

  • Don’t get stuck with the story you started telling. If you keep trying to go back to your first idea, it won’t really work. Instead, use the other person’s “hook” to move on your ideas, which will keep changing each time you add something.
  • Don’t peek at what the other person wrote. It doesn’t matter if it makes sense. In fact, it can be funnier if it doesn’t!

Playdough Recipe

steps.editorState: This no-cook recipe should take you about four minutes to make and keep for around six months! Of course, you could use another recipe or play dough you have bought from a shop instead.

steps.text: Boiling water safety

steps.editorState:
Ingredients:

  • 1 cup plain flour 
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil (baby oil and coconut oil work too) 
  • 1/4 cup salt 
  • 1 tablespoon cream of tartar 
  • 0.5-0.75 cups boiling water (adding in increments until it feels just right) 
  • food colouring (optional) 
  • few drops glycerine (the secret ingredient for extra stretch and shine) (optional) 
  • a sealable bag or box to keep the play dough in when you have finished playing

Method:

  1. Mix the flour, salt, cream of tartar and oil in a mixing bowl. 
  2. Add the foodcolouring (if you are using it) to the hot water and then tip some of the water into the dry ingredients. 
  3. Stir continuously until it becomes a sticky, combined dough, adding more water if it is too dry. 
  4. Add the glycerine, if you are using it. 
  5. Allow it to cool down then take it out of the bowl and knead it vigorously for a couple of minutes until all of the stickiness has gone. The kneading is really important because it's what makes the dough lovely and stretchy. 
  6. If it is still a little sticky then add a bit more flour until it is just right! 
  7. Your playdough is ready to use!

steps.text: In this game, you will be trying to sneak one lie past the other player.

How to Play

  1. Choose a theme each, e.g. 'The Romans' or 'What I did Yesterday'.
  2. Write a paragraph relating to your theme which is all true except for one lie.
  3. Read each other's paragraphs and see if you can spot the lie. If you spot the other person’s lie, you get one point.
  4. Repeat two more times (so you have written three paragraphs each), choosing a new theme each time. The winner is the person with the most points at the end of the three rounds.

What if both players have the same number of points?

Read all the lies again and decide together which was the most creative and interesting. The player who wrote that lie wins!

Writing 1:

Swap bubbles with the other person and write what they said on a piece of paper.
  • If it ends with a ? or ! you can leave it as it is, but if it ends with a full stop you will need to change it to a comma.
  • Add in your speech marks.
  • Write who said it after the speech (and how) – this is called the ‘reporting clause’. Remember, you don't need a capital letter to start the reporting clause when it comes after the speech.
  • Remember to end your sentence with some punctuation too!

Writing 2:

Using the same speech bubbles, see if you can put the reporting clause at the start of the sentence, e.g. Mum shouted, "....."

Preparation:

  1. Cut out two big speech bubbles from the sides of a cereal box.
  2. Each person take one bubble and write something they would say inside the bubble. Remember your capital letter and sentence ending punctuation. Your speech could include more than one sentence if you like.

What to Do:

  1. Open the book (or newspaper or magazine) and find a paragraph.
  2. Read the paragraph aloud.
  3. Talk about these questions together:
    • Is it the first paragraph or does it follow something else?
    • Is there another paragraph after it?
    • How long is it?
    • How does it start?
    • What tense is it written in?
    • How does the second sentence link to the first sentence? Is it with a pronoun or an adverbial or something else?
    • Does the third sentence link back to the second sentence? How?
    • Does the third sentence link back to the first sentence? How?
    • Why did the writer end the paragraph there?

You Will Need:

A text that has paragraphs in it. It could be:
  • A book
  • A newspaper
  • A magazine
  • Something else!

Editing:

Choose one paragraph each. Edit your paragraph so that it all works together. Here are some things to look for:
  • Look for really long sentences which need to be split into several parts.
  • Look for extra words that are not needed when you read the whole sentence.
  • Check that the whole paragraph is written in the same tense (unless there is a good reason it shouldn’t be).
  • Check that the pronouns (he, she, it etc) make sense.
  • Check that singular and plural nouns match the verb they are doing, e.g. one horse runs but two horses run.
  • Think about adding or changing some adverbials to link the sentences together.
  • Decide whether you need to add anything so that it makes sense.

You Will Need:

  • Two things to write with.
  • Two pieces of lined paper (draw your own lines onto plain paper if you need to).

Writing:

  1. Begin writing your paragraph. It can be about anything you like.
  2. When you get to the end of the first line on the page, skip a line and write two more words on the next line.
  3. Fold over the paper so you can’t see the first line of writing but you can still see the two words on the next line.
  4. Swap paper.
  5. Keep writing from the two words you can see. When you get to the end of the line on the page, skip a line again and again write two more words on the next line.
  6. Keep swapping over, writing and folding until you have done ten lines.
  7. Swap one last time, but this time finish the sentence. You can keep going over the end of a line if you need to.
  8. Swap over one last time and unfold the paper. Read your two paragraphs aloud to each other. Did they make you laugh?
This game is about taking it in turns to write lines to make a paragraph. But you won’t see what the person has written before you! It might get silly!

The Activity:

topic.parentName: Where to put ‘said’ when writing speech

steps.text: Answers to Check

Adding the reporting clause (Ben said) at the beginning or end of the speech is the simplest way:

1. Ben said, “Oh no, there’s a tiger! I think it might eat me!”
2. “Oh no, there’s a tiger! I think it might eat me!” Ben said.

You can also add the reporting clause into the middle. This is called interrupted speech. You must make sure the bits either side of ‘Ben said’ still make sense on their own. It is easiest to do this at the end of a sentence:

3. “Oh no, there’s a tiger!” Ben said, “I think it might eat me!”

Another way to make interrupted speech is to use the reporting clause to split a sentence in two, leaving the main clause separate from any extra bits:

4. “Oh no,” Ben said, “There’s a tiger! I think it might eat me!”
5. “Oh no, there’s a tiger! I think,” Ben said, “It might eat me!”

Maybe you also thought of this one. We had to change the punctuation a bit so that it made sense!

6. “Oh…” Ben said, “No! There’s a tiger! I think it might eat me!”
Oh no, there’s a tiger! I think it might eat me!

accidentaly
favorite 		These two are easiest to look up. The beginning of the words looks ok but we’d like to check the middles and endings.

steps.text: Why are we doing this?

This method of checking spellings is really useful if you don't have a dictionary to hand - writing three different spellings in the margin or on a scrap of paper can help you spot the right one because we are better at remembering what looks right than actually how to spell things. You might see adults doing this without thinking, quickly scribbling down a word to check how it's spelled.

Warmup: Find a Word

  1. Player 1 chooses a word from the dictionary/index.
  2. Player 2 must find the word.
  3. Swap over so Player 2 chooses a new word and Player 1 tries to find it.
  4. Repeat three or four times each. Which words were hardest to find?


Activity: Spell a Word

  1. Player 1 finds a word in the dictionary/index and writes it down without showing the other person.
  2. Player 1 tells Player 2 the word but not the spelling.
  3. Player 2 writes down how they think it is spelled.
  4. Player 2 writes down two other possible alternatives, thinking carefully about which phonemes might have alternative spellings.
  5. Player 2 looks at their spellings, chooses the most likely, and looks it up in the dictionary/index.
  6. If it's not there and not easy to spot, can one of the alternative ideas help?
  7. Swap over a few times so you both get several turns.

You Will Need:

  • A dictionary or a book with an index, e.g. a recipe book.
  • A pencil and paper.

steps.text: Brackets can be used for lots of things, but one special purpose is to put in a definition (explaining what a difficult word means). There is an example in that first sentence! Here is another example:
The narcissus (daffodil) is very beautiful.
steps.editorState: The narcissus (daffodil) is very beautiful.

steps.text:
Can you see how the word inside the brackets explains what the word before means? This can be particularly important when writing about something that includes specialist vocabulary – words that not everyone might know the meaning of.

The activity:

  3. In your sentence, put a short explanation in brackets after the tricky word so that people will understand what it means. It is usually best if the explanation is a single word, like ‘daffodil’ in the example, but sometimes you will need to use a few more, like in the first sentence on this page.
  4. Write two more sentences in the same way so you have three sentences all together.

steps.text: Remind me what hyphens are for...

Hyphens can be used to join a prefix to a root word.

This is especially important if the prefix ends in a vowel letter and the root word also begins with one.

For instance, ‘re-enter’ means ‘enter again’ and the hyphen stops it looking like it contains an ‘ee’ sound (‘reenter’ looks really odd).

steps.text: Example Story

steps.editorState:
The Wizard’s Elbow

With a sudden flash, Ringlewald’s second-best tunic burst into flames. He thrust his arm into the nearest oak barrel. Inside, the pink foam stopped swirling and fizzed. The fizzing grew to a slow bubbling. Ringlewald withdrew his arm and retreated. For days he’d been mixing. Nothing had happened yet. Now it worked! He’d succeeded! Bother…

steps.text:
How to Play:

  1. Player 1 starts reading from the book. They could begin at the start or somewhere in the middle. It is probably best to begin at the start of a chapter or section though!
  2. At some point, Player 1 stops reading the actual words in the book and starts making them up.
  3. Player 2 should listen carefully and when they think Player 1 has started making up the words, they call out “Rubbish!”
  4. Player 1 stops talking and you work out the points.
    • Player 1 gets one point for every word of their own they said before Player 2 said, “Rubbish!”
    • Player 2 loses five points if they call out “Rubbish!” before Player 1 has started making up the words.
  5. Make a note of your points so you can see who has won at the end.
  6. Swap over so Player 2 has a chance to read! It is worth playing a few times, because you will find you get better at making up the words after a few goes.
  7. At the end, count up your points to find out who has won!

You Will Need:

  • A book. It can be any book you like! It can also be fun if in each new round, you have a different book.
  • A way of keeping track of your score (e.g. pen and paper or notes on your phone).

Write a story but choose one (or more) of these constraints:
  • Choose one letter and don’t include it anywhere in your story.
  • Write a story exactly 100 words long.
  • Write a story where everything happens within the space of ten minutes.
  • All the characters spend the entire story with their eyes shut.
  • You can’t use the word ‘and’ anywhere in the story.
  • Start by writing the last sentence and work backwards towards the beginning.
  • Electricity doesn’t exist in your story.
  • You can’t use any words less than four letters long.

For this activity, you will need a recipe and the ingredients to cook it.

There are lots of places online where you can find recipes, but one good place is the BBC food website. They have tons of recipes, including a collection called ‘Easy recipes for kids’:
Or you could click the button below to see a recipe for an easy pasta with tomato sauce.

First: Cooking

Follow your recipe to cook some food. This can be a fun thing to do together!

Then: Reflection

When you have finished eating (or while it is cooking), have a look at your recipe and think about how it was organised on the page (on paper or online). Here are some questions to talk about together:
  1. Was the recipe easy to follow? Why (or why not)?
  2. How did the organisation help you to cook it?
  3. How could it have been better organised?
  4. How did the sentence structure help you follow it?
  5. Could it have been written more clearly?
  6. Was your recipe only about the cooking, or was it also written to be interesting to read?

The Activity:

Write your own recipe! It could be for the thing you made in Activity 1, or it could be for something else.

Some things to think about:

  • Who is the recipe for? This is your audience. The recipe will look different if it is for children or adults to follow. It might also look different depending on if it is for adult beginners or people who are more confident.
  • Think about the parts you need to include – what it is, ingredients, equipment etc.
  • Think about how you are going to set your recipe out on the page to make it easy to follow.
  • Think about how to write your sentences. What you choose might depend on your audience – some people will need simpler sentences and some people might be partly reading the recipe for fun and want some more descriptive sections.
When you've finished writing your own recipe (Activity 2), compare it to the one you followed (Activity 1) and decide which you prefer and why.

Here are some questions you could talk about together:

Audience (who they were written for):

  • Who were the recipes written for?
  • What clues do they give about their audience?
  • What special features do they have for their particular audience?
  • Do they fit their audiences or do they need something else to help?


Look on the page:

  • Which recipe looks most attractive on the page? Why?
  • What organisational features do the recipes use?
  • How do the organisational features help the reader?
  • Is it easy to find information? Why or why not?
  • Is it easy to follow the steps in the recipe? Why or why not?


    • Look at the language (word choices) used:

  • Is it formal or informal?
  • Sometimes recipes can be quite chatty, other times they can be bossy, or something else. What are these recipes like?
  • Are there any tricky words? Does the recipe writer explain what they mean? Do they need to explain the words (think about the audience)?
  • Are the words written just to be useful or is there anything to make them fun to read as well as useful to cook?


    • Look at the steps in the recipe:

  • Are the sentences the same length in both recipes? Which is longer?
  • Do the steps contain information that you don’t actually need to be able to cook the recipe? Why? Is it helpful or unhelpful?
  • How do the steps begin – are there sentence openers? How do they help?


    • Deciding which you prefer:

    • Which recipe do you prefer? Why?
    • Do you think everyone would like the same one as you? Why?
    • Who might prefer the other one?

Find somewhere comfy to sit and listen to a story! Reading a real book is good because it is easy to stop, look at the pictures and talk about what is happening. But for this activity, you could use a story in another format. Here are some suggestions:

  • A book from home, school or the library;
  • A YouTube reading of a story;
  • A story on CBeebies Radio;
  • An audiobook from the library;
  • Tell a story you know without using a book.

Top Tips:

  • Make sure you can both see/hear the story so you can both listen and talk about it.
  • Let your child turn the pages (if you’re using a book) – this lets them really look at the pictures and move through the story at their own pace.
  • Encourage them to talk about the pictures – you can ask if they can see something specific in the picture, or let them tell you about it.
  • When you have finished the story, you can ask them if they liked it and if they had a favourite character.

Top Tips:

• Don’t read any of the words. Instead, move through the book at whatever speed your child wants, talking about the pictures as you go.

  • Make a den by putting a cloth or blanket over a table and have your story in the den.
  • Use mini figures to act out a story you know.
  • Dress up as characters from a story.

Playdough Recipe

steps.editorState: This no-cook recipe should take you about four minutes to make and keep for around six months! Of course, you could use another recipe or play dough you have bought from a shop instead.

steps.text: Boiling water safety

steps.editorState:
Ingredients:

  • 1 cup plain flour 
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil (baby oil and coconut oil work too) 
  • 1/4 cup salt 
  • 1 tablespoon cream of tartar 
  • 0.5-0.75 cups boiling water (adding in increments until it feels just right) 
  • food colouring (optional) 
  • few drops glycerine (the secret ingredient for extra stretch and shine) (optional) 
  • a sealable bag or box to keep the play dough in when you have finished playing

Method:

  1. Mix the flour, salt, cream of tartar and oil in a mixing bowl. 
  2. Add the foodcolouring (if you are using it) to the hot water and then tip some of the water into the dry ingredients. 
  3. Stir continuously until it becomes a sticky, combined dough, adding more water if it is too dry. 
  4. Add the glycerine, if you are using it. 
  5. Allow it to cool down then take it out of the bowl and knead it vigorously for a couple of minutes until all of the stickiness has gone. The kneading is really important because it's what makes the dough lovely and stretchy. 
  6. If it is still a little sticky then add a bit more flour until it is just right! 
  7. Your playdough is ready to use!

steps.text: Some Ideas

• Use a plastic knife to cut zigzags;
  • Use the blunt end of a pencil to make dots;
  • Use plastic animals to make footprints;
  • Press pasta shapes into the dough;
  • See how many different marks one object can make, depending how you push it into the playdough;
  • Make shapes with a piece of string and pushing it into the dough.

How to Play:

  • Pick a phoneme that could be at the start of a word, e.g. 'ch'.
  • Say "Find something beginning with…" and say your phoneme, .e.g "Find something beginning with 'ch'".

  • Take it in turns to give the clue.


What is a Phoneme?

A phoneme is one of the sounds that makes up a word, e.g. the word 'chip' has three phonemes: 'ch', 'i' and 'p'.

Textured letter shapes: 'e' rice, 'f' sandpaper, 's' buttons, and 'j' crinkly card.

Raised lines

Trace the line with glue (let it dry before you start writing).

Indented lines

Making a dip along the line can help to feel where it is. You could do this by:
  • Putting another piece of paper and drawing over the line, pressing down really hard with a biro. This will leave a dent on the lined paper underneath.
  • Making little holes along the line from the back of the paper by poking a pin through (it could be quicker to use a sewing machine with no thread in).

Coloured lines

This is the easiest – trace over the line using a yellow pen or highlighter!

The letters e f s and j are some of the hardest to place on the line when writing because they all start in slightly funny places. Changing the line in different ways can help with getting the letters in the correct place!

Playdough Recipe

steps.editorState:
Method:

  1. Mix the flour, salt, cream of tartar and oil in a mixing bowl. 
  2. Add the foodcolouring (if you are using it) to the hot water and then tip some of the water into the dry ingredients. 
  3. Stir continuously until it becomes a sticky, combined dough, adding more water if it is too dry. 
  4. Add the glycerine, if you are using it. 
  5. Allow it to cool down then take it out of the bowl and knead it vigorously for a couple of minutes until all of the stickiness has gone. The kneading is really important because it's what makes the dough lovely and stretchy. 
  6. If it is still a little sticky then add a bit more flour until it is just right! 
  7. Your playdough is ready to use!

Ingredients:

  • 1 cup plain flour 
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil (baby oil and coconut oil work too) 
  • 1/4 cup salt 
  • 1 tablespoon cream of tartar 
  • 0.5-0.75 cups boiling water (adding in increments until it feels just right) 
  • food colouring (optional) 
  • few drops glycerine (the secret ingredient for extra stretch and shine) (optional) 
  • a sealable bag or box to keep the play dough in when you have finished playing
This no-cook recipe should take you about four minutes to make and keep for around six months! Of course, you could use another recipe or play dough you have bought from a shop instead.

The Game:

Players take it in turns to add things to the list of what King Henry ate at the banquet.
  • Each player starts their turn by saying ‘At the banquet, King Henry ate...’
  • Players add a new food to the end of the list on every turn.
  • You must remember all the foods already in the list and say them before you add a new one.
  • Try to only say ‘and’ before the last food in the list (not between all the foods).
  • Say ‘comma’ and do the kung fu comma action between all the foods in the list (except for when you say ‘and’).

Player 1: At the banquet, King Henry ate pies.
Player 2: At the banquet, King Henry ate pies and soup.
Player 1: At the banquet, King Henry ate pies COMMA soup and cake.
Player 2: At the banquet, King Henry ate pies COMMA soup COMMA cake and a whole peacock.

Before You Start:

Cut out your cards and click the button below for a reminder about apostrophes for contraction.

Short of Space?

You could try using the same cards to play snap. Pile the cards face down and take it in turns to turn over a card. Each time you turn one over, read what is on it and say what it’s pair would be (like in the Memory Card game).

You Will Need:

Word cards (click the download below if you have not been sent home cards from school).

The Activity:

  1. Spread the cards face down on the table.
  2. Player 1 turns over one card and reads what is on it, e.g. “it’s”
  3. Player 1 then says what other card they are hoping for, e.g. “it is” if they already turned over “it’s”.
  4. Player 1 turns over a second card. If it goes with their first card, they keep both and have another turn. If it doesn’t match, they turn both cards back over and it is Player 2’s turn.
  5. Take it in turns to turn over cards until all the cards are gone. The person with the most cards at the end is the winner!
Apostrophes for Contraction

What does an apostrophe look like?

An apostrophe looks like a comma but floating in the air between two letters. Here's one!

What are apostrophes for?

There are several ways apostrophes can be used. In these activities, we are looking at apostrophes that show a letter or letters are missing.

Examples of apostrophes where a letter or letters are missing:
it’s → it is
don’t → do not
she’s → she is
can’t → cannot

And one slightly odd one…
won’t → will not
The English language and spelling has changed over time, and “won’t” is actually short for “woll not”. We say “will not” now, but the old spelling has stuck in the short version “won’t”.

Why is this called 'contraction'?

Because 'contraction' means 'becoming smaller' - the words become smaller when the letters are missed out and an apostrophe is used instead.

You Will Need:

The same word cards as in Activity 1 (click the button below)

How to Play

  1. Stack up the cards face down.
  2. Player 1 picks the top card and says a sentence with its other version, e.g. pick "it's" and say "It is raining."
  3. Player 2 takes the next card and says a sentence with its other version, e.g. pick "they are" and say "They’re going to the shops.”
  4. Repeat until all the cards are gone.

steps.text: Things to Watch Out For

• Check the correct letters are missing and that the apostrophe is in their space.
  • Check that the apostrophe is this way round: ’
  • Check that the apostrophe is high up in the word, level with the top of tall letters like l or h.
  • Check that the dot of the apostrophe is just a dot and not a big blob.

Challenge Rules:

Then decide what letters are missing in the short version. Rub them out and write an apostrophe in the space to show letters are missing.

There are several ways apostrophes can be used. In these activities, we are looking at apostrophes that show something belongs to someone.

The Activity:

Make labels that tell you who things belong to and put them on the things around your house!
  1. Think about who it belongs to, e.g. Mum.
  2. Write their name on your label.
  3. Write ’s after their name, e.g. Mum’s
  4. Write the thing after that, e.g. Mum’s shoes.


Top Tips:

  • Make sure your apostrophe is the same shape as a comma – a little dot with a short, curly tail.
  • Make sure your apostrophe is floating in the air at about the same height as tall letters and capital letters.
  • Make sure the word with the apostrophe in still looks like a word – give the apostrophe some room but not big spaces like finger spaces!

The Activity:

The Activity:

Look at the pictures on the sheet. Each picture includes a thing that belongs to a person or animal. Write a sentence to go with each picture which includes a word with an apostrophe to show who the thing belongs to.

You Will Need:

  • A bowl (or other container, e.g. a hat or bag)
  • Ten scraps of paper each

Setting Up:

On each of your ten pieces of paper, write down a character or famous person you both know about. Fold each piece of paper in half and put it in the bowl.

How to Play:

Take it in turns to pick out one pieces of paper and pretend to be that person for the other player to guess.

Challenge:

Give yourself a time limit and see how many the other person can guess in the time.

Some Ideas:

  • Cook dinner together pretending to be Daddy Bear and Baby Bear.
  • Tidy up together pretending to be Spiderman and Batman.
  • Clean the car together pretending to be Rapunzel and Maximus.
  • Hang out the washing together pretending to be the Big Bad Wolf and Little Red Riding Hood.

The Activity:

Choose a character each and do something together around the house.

What to Do:

  1. Read the poem aloud and talk together about what is happening. It’s much easier to perform if you know what is going on!
  2. Read it aloud some more times, thinking about making the words flow (this is called being ‘fluent’).
  3. When you are reading, think about how to make the poem interesting to listen to:
    • Can you do different voices for different characters?
    • Might different parts need to be louder or quieter?
    • Anything else? You decide!
  4. When you’ve finished practising, perform your poem. You could perform to someone in your house, on a video call to family somewhere else, or record your performance.
Have a go at performing a poem. You can choose your own or use the one by clicking the button below.
How to Write a 'Looking Closely' Poem

1. Choose an object. It can be anything – a pebble you collected, a button, something special, or something ordinary.
  2. Look at it really closely. What do you see?
  3. Write down what you can see. Try to get every detail!
  4. Remember, poems don’t need to rhyme. This kind of poem will probably look like a list of sentences, and that’s ok!

steps.text:
What should I write?

You can write absolutely anything, but if you want an idea to get started, try this:

Performing the Poem:

  • Remember to practise first – say the words out loud lots of times so you can say them smoothly and clearly. This is called being ‘fluent’.
  • Think about how to change your voice while you are reading. Maybe some of the words need to be louder or quieter, faster or slower.
  • When you’ve finished practising, perform your poem to the other person!

The Activity:

Have a go at writing your own poem and then performing it. It can be fun for both of you to write a poem so you can perform them to each other at the end.

Setting Up:

  1. Decide what story you are going to tell. It could be a story you know or one you are making up. But the inside of the box needs to match your story!
  2. Make sure your box has a hole at the front. A shoe box comes like this, but you might need to cut a hole in the side of a cereal box.
  3. Decorate the box. You can draw or stick things on the back, on the bottom and hanging down the front!
  4. Put your characters into your box.


Practise:

Practise moving the characters around and saying words to tell the story. You might want to use your own voice as the narrator as well as making the characters speak.

Perform:

When you have finished practising, find an audience to perform to. It could be someone in your house or you could even set up an audience of teddies to perform to!
Scissor Safety
Children learn to use children’s scissors safely in school. Please supervise children carefully when using scissors, or cut things yourself if scissors are large and sharp.

Talk to them about:

- Always using the handles properly when using scissors

- Always cutting away from yourself and others.

- Never running with scissors.

- Put scissors down when not in use.

- If you walk with scissors, hold them with the blade down.

You Will Need:

  • A shoe box (or other similar sized box, e.g. a cereal box)
  • Things to decorate the inside with. You could use:
    • Old wrapping paper
    • Food packaging
    • Stickers
    • Toys

    • Colouring pens and pencils

steps.text: Playdough Recipe
Boiling water safety

steps.editorState:
Ingredients:

  • 1 cup plain flour 
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil (baby oil and coconut oil work too) 
  • 1/4 cup salt 
  • 1 tablespoon cream of tartar 
  • 0.5-0.75 cups boiling water (adding in increments until it feels just right) 
  • food colouring (optional) 
  • few drops glycerine (the secret ingredient for extra stretch and shine) (optional) 
  • a sealable bag or box to keep the play dough in when you have finished playing
This no-cook recipe should take you about four minutes to make and keep for around six months! Of course, you could use another recipe or play dough you have bought from a shop instead.

Method:

  1. Mix the flour, salt, cream of tartar and oil in a mixing bowl. 
  2. Add the foodcolouring (if you are using it) to the hot water and then tip some of the water into the dry ingredients. 
  3. Stir continuously until it becomes a sticky, combined dough, adding more water if it is too dry. 
  4. Add the glycerine, if you are using it. 
  5. Allow it to cool down then take it out of the bowl and knead it vigorously for a couple of minutes until all of the stickiness has gone. The kneading is really important because it's what makes the dough lovely and stretchy. 
  6. If it is still a little sticky then add a bit more flour until it is just right! 
  7. Your playdough is ready to use!

Here are some examples: 'The dog jumped'; 'Dad snored'; 'The girl ran as fast as her legs would carry her'; 'Grandma was the funniest person he had ever met'; 'Once upon a time, there was a little boy called Robin'."}} , the Joiner says another conjunction.

steps.text:
How to Play:

  1. Choose a five-syllable word.
  2. Tell the other player the first syllable.
  3. They guess a word. They get five points if they are correct.
  4. If they are incorrect, tell them the second syllable. Four points if correct.
  5. If incorrect, tell them the third syllable. Two points if correct.
  6. If incorrect, tell them the fourth syllable. One point if correct.
  7. If incorrect, tell them the whole word! They get zero points.
  8. Swap over a few times so you both get several goes at guessing the word.


What Word Should I Choose?

Here are some ideas:
In this game, you need to guess the word chosen by the other player by thinking carefully about how it starts!
A koala is thinking.
In this game, players win points by listing things in different categories.
Example List It Game!

Let’s play five rounds.

Round 1:

Our category is Disney films.

Bidding:
  • Player 1: I can name four films.
  • Player 2: Raise – I can do five films.
  • Player 1: Raise – I can do six.
  • Player 2: Raise – eight!
  • Player 1: I can’t do more than eight! I pull out. You can try eight!
Player 2 won the bidding!

Listing:
Because Player 2 won the bidding with eight, they have two minutes to name eight Disney films.
  1. Mulan
  2. Brave
  3. Frozen
  4. Tangled
  5. Lion King
  6. Tarzan
  7. Cinderella
  8. …
Unfortunately, Player 2 only managed to name seven Disney films, so Player 1 gets one point! (Player 2 would have got three points if they had thought of eight).

Round 2:

Choose a new category, make your bids, and do your list!

Keep playing until you have done all five rounds, then see who has the most points!

How to Play:

  1. Decide how many rounds you want to play.
    Five can be a good number.
  2. Choose a category (specific or general but not too broad).
    E.g. car brands, Harry Potter novels, cow breeds, English counties…
  3. Take it in turns to bid how many you think you can name.
    If you are not sure how to bid, see the example below!
  4. The person who makes the highest bid gets two minutes to name as many as they can.
  5. If they say the same number or more than they bid, they get, 3 points. If they don't, the other player gets 1 point.
  6. Choose a new category for each new round.
  7. The person with most points at the end of all the rounds wins!
Other Rules for Giving Clues

• The clues must be about the meaning of the words, not the spelling or where it is in the grid.
  • You can use letters and numbers for clues if they relate to the meaning, e.g. ‘eight’ could be a clue for ‘octopus’ but not for eight-letter words.
  • You can’t say any form of a word visible on the grid, e.g. if ‘run’ is on the grid, you can’t say ‘run’, ‘running’, ‘ran’ etc until after the word ‘run’ is covered by a counter.
  • You also can’t say part of a compound word in the grid, e.g. if the word ‘blackbird’ is in the grid, you can’t say ‘bird’, ‘birdie’ or ‘songbird’.
  • You must use words that are regularly used in English sentences.

You Will Need:

  • A 4x6 playing grid with words on.
  • A card showing you 9 target words and 3 poison words to avoid.
  • Two colours of counters to cover words you have guessed.
    • Call one set of counters ‘target counters’ and one set of counters ‘other counters’.
    • You could use two types of coin, buttons, pasta or anything you like.

The Aim of the Game:

Player 1 gives single-word clues for the target words and Player 2 tries to guess them in as few turns as possible without accidentally choosing any of the other words. If Player 2 guesses a poison word, the game ends!

How to Play

  1. Put a word grid on the table or floor between you.
  2. Player 1 looks at a target word card to see which words are target words, which words they should avoid, and which are the three poison words. They must not show the card to Player 2.
  3. Player 1 gives a single-word clue that relates to some of the target words. Player 1 also gives a number to say how many words relate to the clue. E.g. two of your words are ‘sand’ and ‘sea’ and both of these are part of a beach, so you say, ‘Beach: 2.’
  4. Player 2 thinks about the clue and talks about their thinking out loud. Player 1 is not allowed to say anything or give any face or movement hints to help. Listening to Player 2 is useful though, as it can help you understand their thinking ready for giving the next clue.
  5. When Player 2 has decided on a word (or words), they touch one word on the grid.
    • If it was a target word, put a 'target counter' on the word. Player 2 may guess another word (up to the number given by Player 1 in the clue).
    • If it was a poison word, the game ends.
    • If it was another word, put an ‘other counter’ on the word. The turn ends.
  6. On the next turn, Player 1 gives a new clue.
  7. Keep track of how many clues are given before all the target words are found.
  8. At the end of the game, add together your number of clues given and the number of ‘other words’ accidentally guessed. This is your score for the game. The lower the score, the better! If you accidentally guessed a poison word, the game ended with a high score of infinity!
  9. Play again but swapping roles so the other person has a chance to give the clues. See if you can beat your score!


Important Rule:

The player giving the clues is not allowed to help in any other way – they can’t comment on their own clues (e.g. ‘this is maybe a bit of a stretch), they can’t comment on the other player’s choices, they can’t even move their face!!
This game is like the ordinary game of I-Spy, but instead of saying what you can see, you say where you can see something.
Here are some clues you could give for <u>grass</u> if you were in the park in the photo:

I spy with my little eye something under something beginning with T.
The bench is under a tree. Is it bench?
No, it’s not bench. I spy with my little eye something next to something beginning with B.
There are leaves next to the bin. Is it leaves?
No, it’s not leaves. I spy with my little eye something beside something beginning with P.
There is grass beside the path. Is it grass?
Yes, it is grass!

The words in bold in the example are called ‘prepositions’. You will need to use one in every clue. Here are some examples (you might know more):
  • In
  • Beside
  • Under
  • Behind
  • On
  • Above
  • Below
  • Opposite
  • Next to
  • Near


Don’t forget, in this version of I Spy, you can use a different letter for every clue. Just choose a new preposition each time!
Prepositions can be used to describe when, where and why something happened. In this activity, you will practise using all three.
Example Prepositions Game

In this example, the question words are in blue, the verb is in green and the prepositions are in orange:

  1. Player 1 asks: “What did you do today?”
  2. Player 2 answers with a verb, e.g. “I ran.”
  3. Player 1 asks: “When did you run?”
  4. Player 2 answers, e.g. “I ran at playtime,” or “I ran in the morning.”
  5. Player 1 asks: “Where did you run?”
  6. Player 2 answers, e.g. “I ran around the playground,” or “I ran down the corridor.”
  7. Player 1 asks: “Why did you run?”
  8. Player 2 answers, e.g. “I ran because of the lion chasing me,” or “I ran due to the rain.”
  9. Swap over so that Player 2 can ask the questions.


Note:
In step 8, if you choose ‘because’ it’s really important to say ‘because of’ not just ‘because’. This is so that you are using a preposition – if you leave out ‘of’, ‘because’ might be working as a conjunction instead.

What to Do:

  • Player 1 asks four questions for player 2 to answer. These questions begin with:
    • what
    • when
    • where
    • why
  • Player 2 answers the first question with a verb and the other three using whole sentences that include prepositions.

What to Do:

  1. Choose a die and roll it to get a preposition.
  2. Say the preposition in a sentence.
  3. Write down the sentence.
  4. Repeat so that you have written three sentences.

Top Tips:

Remember, prepositions can be used at the beginning of a sentence as well as in the middle.

steps.text:
How to play:

  1. Player 1 thinks of a person both players know. You must really know them (you can’t use a famous person) because it really helps if you know them really well.
  2. Player 2 asks questions to help them find out which person Player 1 is thinking of. But all the questions must use metaphors. Here are some examples:
    • What colour are they?
    • What animal are they?
    • What taste are they?
    • What film are they?
    • What biscuit are they?
    • What chair are they?
  3. Player 1 answers the question, thinking carefully about what the person is really like. Player 1 must say a one-word answer. Here’s an example:
    • Player 1 thinks: Grandma.
    • Player 2 says: What chair are they?
    • Player 1 thinks: If Grandma was a chair, she’d be a sofa because she’s comforting, and it feels safe and cosy being with her.
    • Player 1 says: Sofa
  4. Player 2 keeps asking questions until they feel sure they know who it is. It’s best to ask a few more questions after you think you know so that you can be really certain!
