steps.text: How do maths games help with learning?

steps.editorState:
Fun

Games can be an enjoyable, motivating way to practice a skill many times.

Positive feelings

Having fun together encourages positive feelings towards maths and can reduce worry about making mistakes.

Memory

Skills that are practiced when a child is fully engaged and relaxed are more likely to be remembered.

Number sense

In trying to win, children really think about the numbers they choose. This builds number sense - a deeper, more flexible understanding of numbers.

Problem solving

Finding strategies to win develops problem solving skills.

Mathematical Vocabulary

Talking about a game or explaining it to someone else encourages children to use mathematical vocabulary.

Deeper thinking

Changing a rule and talking about how that impacts a game encourages an even deeper level of thinking.

carouselData.textEditorState: Where does the word “Monday” come from?
It is from the Old English “Monandæg,” meaning “Moon’s day.”
The Anglo-Saxons based their word on the Latin “Dies Lunae”, which translates to “day of the Moon,” where “Luna” means “Moon.”
The Romans (who spoke Latin) didn’t invent the names of the days. Their calendar is actually influenced by even older cultures, including the Ancient Babylonians.
The Babylonians also had a seven day week, and they named Monday “The Day of the Moon” (𒌓𒌓𒌅).

steps.text: What we thought

steps.editorState:
Why is this?

When the Normans invaded England in 1066, they spoke French. The people already living in England spoke a different language: Anglo-Saxon.

The Normans became the rulers and the Anglo-Saxons were there servants. The servants cared for the animals and the rulers ate the meat. 

Over time, these languages have combined with each other (and other things) to become modern English. We have kept both words because they came to mean slightly different things - the animals in the fields and the food on our plates.
The words we use for animals come from Anglo-Saxon and the words we use for meat come from French.

Choose something to hit with your sticks.

This game will help your child to learn their left and right.

What to do:

  • Stand next to each other, not face to face.
  • Make up a set of actions, or a dance, using left and right.

steps.text: Some more ways to practice left and right.

steps.editorState:
• Ask your child to set the table - knife on the right, fork on the left.
  • Put stickers with R and L inside their shoes.
  • Talk about which hand they write with.
  • Work out which foot they prefer to kick a ball with.
  • Use left and right when asking your child for things - can you pass me the glass on the right.
  • Name your feet as you walk or climb the stairs or march - left foot, right foot.
  • Use something to help them recognise one hand - a bracelet, painted fingernail or temporary tattoo.
  • Play games like Simon Says with actions using left and right.
  • Ask your child which way to turn when walking or driving a familiar route.
  • Sing the Hokey Cokey song together.

steps.editorState:
What to do:

Roll the dice and follow the instructions

Extra Challenge:

Make this a game of Simon Says

Only do the action if the instruction starts with 'Simon says . ."

For example:

"Simon Says make a quarter turn" - do the action

"Simon Says make a whole turn" - do the action

"Make a half turn" - don't do the action!

What to do:

Make some patterns which use turns.

  • You can draw around an object, but turn it each time.
  • You can use a set of toys like lego people.
  • You can collect sticks or leaves outside.

steps.text: Leaves arranged in a pattern with quarter turns

steps.editorState:
You'll need:

Pens and paper

or

Toys

or

Natural objects like leaves

Extra challenge:

Take it in turns to start a pattern.

Can the other person continue it?

Extra Challenge:

Talk about clockwise and anti-clockwise turns.

Take it in turns to give eachother instructions with these phrases.

For example: Make a half turn clockwise.

What to do:

Try an activity to help your child link turns with telling the time:

  • Encourage your child to spot times with halves and quarters - o'clock, quarter past, half past and quarter to.
  • Talk about specific times in your daily routine - "We can play until quarter past 4"
  • Notice which way clock hands always turn. 
  • Practice making different times on a toy clock or paper clock.
  • Play any board or card games you have with clocks.

steps.text: What is mime?

steps.editorState:
Mime is when you use your face and your body to act out a story. You don't use any sound, and you don't need any objects.

For instance, you would mime carrying a heavy bag by pretending to pick up an invisible bag, making sure you move slowly to show how heavy it is, and using your face to show that it is hard work.

You'll need:

A stopwatch - there's one here or one on a smartphone!

steps.editorState:
Extra Challenge:

Can you extimate how long something will take BEFORE you do it?

Extra Challenge:

Count how many hours your child spends doing different activites in a day

For example:

  • How many hours asleep each night.
  • How many hours in school.
  • How many hours playing.

This is a talking activity to help your child understand how long an hour is.

What to do:

1) Together, think of different things you do that take about an hour.

For example - a club or activty, the journey to see a grandparent or a TV programme.

2) Think of things that take more than an hour.

3) Think of things that take less than an hour.

And the elephants?

One way to count seconds is to say 'one elephant, two elephants . . .'

Finding it tricky?

Try counting a shorter time, like 10 seconds.

• First practice counting seconds with the clock.
  • You can count elephants, or choose another word.
  • Then, close your eyes and count up to 60 together.
  • Open your eyes.
  • How close did you get to one minute?

Extra fun:

Give each other activities to do for one minute.

steps.editorState: The suffix 'ation' is added at the end of {{definition "verbs" "Verbs are doing words, e.g. 'run' or 'clap'."}} to form {{definition "nouns" "Nouns are the names of things, e.g. 'car' or 'octopus'."}} . This game is all about thinking about what the nouns mean.

steps.text: A child koala explaining something to an adult koala.

Cancellation - something that has been cancelled and will no longer happen, e.g. a bus journey.
Commendation - a piece of formal or official praise.

Desertification - the process of an area of land turning into a desert.
Duration - the length of time something lasts.

Electrification - the process of making something electric, e.g. a railway.
Exhalation - the process of breathing out.
Experimentation - the process of doing an experiment.
Exploitation - the act of treating someone unfairly in order to benefit from their work.

Generalisation - a general statement that can be applied to lots of things based on a specific case.

Hospitalisation - the process of becoming ill or injured in a way that means you have to go into hospital.

Information - facts about something.
Improvisation - the act of making something up on the spot.
Inspiration - the process of being mentally stimulated to do something, especially something creative.

Nationalisation - the process of becoming run by the nation or government.

Objectification - the action of making a person seem less valuable by treating them like an object.
Organisation - an organised group of people who are together for a purpose, e.g. a business. 

Perspiration - another word for sweat.
Prioritisation - the process of deciding which things are more important to do first.

Respiration - the process of gases being used by an animal or plant to create energy.

Starvation - the suffering caused by a serious lack of food.

Temptation - the desire to do something, particularly something wrong or unwise.
Transplantation - the process of moving a plant to a new piece of soil or an organ to a new body, e.g. a kidney transplant.
Transportation - the process of moving something from one place to another.

Valuation - an estimation of how much money something is worth.

How to play:

  1. Roll the two dice below to get two words ending 'ation'.
  2. Player 1 chooses one of the words and explains what it means (you can check the meaning below if you need to).
  3. Player 2 guesses which word they chose.
  4. When Player 2 has guessed the word correctly, they roll that die again to get one new word.
  5. Player 2 now chooses one of the two words for Player 1 to guess.
  6. Repeat!

  4. When Player 2 has guessed the word correctly, they roll that die again to get one new word.
  5. Player 2 now chooses one of the two words for Player 1 to guess.

steps.text: How to convert miles to kilometers

steps.editorState:
There are different ways to convert miles to kilometres.

1. Using a formula

We know 1 mile is approximately 1.6km

So multiply the number of miles by 1.6 to give the number of km.

For example: 6 miles is 6 x 1.6 = 9.6km

We also know that 1km is approximately 0.6 miles.

So multiply the number of kilometers by 0.6

For example: 5 km x 0.6 = 3 miles.

2. Using key facts

You can use the key fact that 5 miles is approximately 8km.

So 10 miles is approximately 16 km.  

20 miles is 32 km

100 miles is 160 km etc . .

steps.text: Answering children's questions

steps.editorState:
• Money is a sensitive subject.
  • All families have different ideas about what they want to talk to children about.
  • These activities are designed to start conversations - but it is up to you to decide what to tell children.
  • Children are curious - and have no idea that some questions might be too personal.
  • There is no need to talk about anything you don't want to.
  • This may be a good opportunity to teach them how to talk about money politely and sensitively.
  • Asking a question back can be a good way to return the conversation back to them.

Deflecting tricky questions

It can sometimes be tricky when children ask question that you don't feel comfortable answering.

Here are some possible responses:

Q: How much money do you have?

How much money people have is usually something they keep private.  

It's also quite complicated for grown ups - it changes all the time so there isn't a simple answer.

Adults bank accounts can also be complicated. You can have different accounts for different things.

We have enough money for what we need.  

Questions to ask back:

  • What do you think adults need to pay for with their money?  
  • Do you know how much money you have in your money box? 
  • Can you think of good ways to keep track of how much money you have?
  • Why do you think adults keep money in bank accounts and not in money boxes?

Q: How much do you earn?

People's salaries are often private. Exact amounts are not something people usually share.  

When you are talking to people, they may think it was rude to ask them about how much they earn.  

There isn't one number to say how much you are paid as money is taken off for Tax and Pensions and National Insurance and Student loan payments before you even get it.

I earn more now than I did when I worked at . . because I have more responsiblity and have to work at the weekends more.

I earn less now that I did when I worked at . . but I have more time at home with you and don't have to travel as far.

Questions to ask back:

  • What kind of job would you like to do? Why?
  • Which do you think will be more important to you - salary, a good work-life balance or doing a job you enjoy?

You will need:

  • A hat, bowl, or other container to put your words in;
  • A piece of paper torn or cut into pieces to write words on (it can be scrap paper, e.g. part of an old envelope);
  • A pen or pencil;
  • A one minute timer (you can use the one at the bottom of this page).

How to play:

  1. Player 1 has one minute to describe as many of the words from the container as they can for Player 2 to guess. 
  2. Player 1 should keep any words that are guessed. Return any un-guessed words to the container.
  3. When the time runs out, swap over. Now Player 2 has one minute to describe as many of the words from the container as they can for Player 2 to guess. 
  4. Player 2 should keep any words that are guessed. Return any un-guessed words to the container. 
  5. Keep taking it in turns to describe words until there are no words left.
  6. The winner is the player who described the most words!

Getting ready:

Use twelve scraps of paper each. Both players should write:

  • The names of four famous people
  • Four other {{definition "nouns" "Nouns are things like objects, e.g. 'horse', 'apple' or 'love'."}}
  • Four {{definition "verbs" "Verbs are doing words, e.g. 'running' or 'flying'."}}

Fold all the pieces of paper in half, and put them in your container.

steps.editorState:
Ball in the long grass

All our legs are swishing through the grasses in the park

Where did the ball go?

Ted, the dog, crashes through the undergrowth

But he's found a squirrel not the ball

And as he barks his way into the bushes

The squirrel rushes upwards and bounds away through the branches

Which sway and rustle as it passes.

Little sister Mina is toddling round in circles

The grass almost up to her chin

Chuckling as the tops tickle

Giggling as she bustles on

Ball completely forgotten.

But I haven't forgotten

And I saw how we kicked the ball

And it soared high in the clear blue sky

And fell with a thud in the grass just over there

So I push my way on through the swishing grass.

And when I see it lying there, I grab it,

And hoof it back into the game.

steps.text: Not sure how to start?

steps.editorState:
You can do anything you like, but you could start like this:

  1. Choose a noisy place you know, e.g. the street on the way to school.
  2. Make a plan by writing down some noises you would hear there, e.g. honking horns, rumbling engines, children calling to their friends.
  3. Do you want a first introduction line for your poem? You could start "The walk to school is noisy".
  4. Add in your sounds - you could just make a list of all the sounds you hear, or you could add other things between the sounds.
  5. Think about how to end your poem. It could be getting more and more noisy, or you might want the silence as the whistle blows to go into school. You choose!

Where's the learning?

steps.editorState:
There is lot of learning here, including:

  • To experience spending money in the real world.
  • To understand how money is exchanged for things.
  • To understand that different items have different prices.
  • To build confidence speaking to other adults.

steps.text: How does this help?

steps.editorState:
A magic sounds box helps children to:

  • Listen carefully,
  • Enjoy playing together,
  • Have fun making different sounds with you.

How to play:

  1. Sit opposite your child, holding the box. 
  2. The box becomes ‘magic’ when you turn it around in your hand, saying the rhyme:
    Turn, turn, turn the box round,
    Lift the lid and listen for the sound!
  3. Point to your ear as you say ‘listen’. 
  4. As you open the lid, make a sound with your voice that matches one of the objects. Keep the sound going (with the lid in front of our mouth) until you shut the lid, to extend the magic! 
  5. Can your child guess the sound? Can they make the sounds with you?

You will need:

  • A small box with a lid (ideally a flap lid, e.g. teabag or laundry powder tablet boxes are good). You can decorate the box if you are feeling creative!
  • Small objects or pictures of things that would make a sound (e.g. toy animals or vehicles) to put inside the box.

steps.text: Where's the learning?

steps.editorState:
There is lot of learning here, including:

  • To experience spending money in the real world.
  • To experience making a choice themselves.
  • To understand that different items have different prices.
  • To understand the idea of having enough money.
  • To build confidence speaking to other adults.

Don't worry if your child needs lots of help the first time they do this.

The focus is on the experience rather than the maths.

There is no need for your child to add up several items or calculate change themselves.

steps.text: A child paying in a supermarket

steps.editorState:
What to do:

Help your child to make a choice in a shop.

  1. Give them a small amount of money to spend.
  2. Talk to them about the choices they can make.
  3. Together look at the prices on different items.
  4. Help them to check if they have enough money.
  5. Ask your child to take the money and the item to the till.
  6. Let them do the buying, take any change and the receipt.

steps.text: The story

steps.editorState:
1. What! No Children?

Once upon a time, so long ago that I have quite forgotten the date, there lived a king and queen who had no children.

And the king said to himself, “All the queens of my acquaintance have children, some three, some seven, and some as many as twelve; and my queen has not one. I feel ill-used.” So he made up his mind to be cross with his wife about it. But she bore it all like a good patient queen as she was. Then the king grew very cross indeed. But the queen pretended to take it all as a joke, and a very good one too.

“Why don’t you have any daughters, at least?” said he. “I don’t say sons; that might be too much to expect.”

“I am sure, dear king, I am very sorry,” said the queen.

“So you ought to be,” retorted the king, “You are not going to make a virtue of that, surely.”

But he was not an ill-tempered king, and in any matter of less moment would have let the queen have her own way with all his heart. This, however, was an affair of state.

The queen smiled. “You must have patience with a lady, you know, dear king,” said she.

She was, indeed, a very nice queen, and heartily sorry that she could not oblige the king immediately.

2. Won’t I, Just?

The king tried to have patience, but he succeeded very badly. It was more than he deserved, therefore, when, at last, the queen gave him a daughter—as lovely a little princess as ever cried. The day drew near when the infant must be christened. The king wrote all the invitations with his own hand. Of course somebody was forgotten. Now it does not generally matter if somebody is forgotten, only you must mind who. Unfortunately, the king forgot without intending to forget; and so the chance fell upon the Princess Makemnoit, which was awkward. For the princess was the king’s own sister; and he ought not to have forgotten her. But she had made herself so disagreeable to the old king, their father, that he had forgotten her in making his will; and so it was no wonder that her brother forgot her in writing his invitations. But poor relations don’t do anything to keep you in mind of them. Why don’t they? The king could not see into the garret she lived in, could he? She was a sour, spiteful creature. The wrinkles of contempt crossed the wrinkles of peevishness and made her face as full of wrinkles as a pat of butter. If ever a king could be justified in forgetting anybody, this king was justified in forgetting his sister, even at a christening. She looked very odd, too. Her forehead was as large as all the rest of her face and projected over it like a precipice. When she was angry, her little eyes flashed blue. When she hated anybody, they shone yellow and green. What they looked like when she loved anybody, I do not know; for I never heard of her loving anybody but herself, and I do not think she could have managed that if she had not somehow got used to herself. But what made it highly imprudent in the king to forget her was that she was awfully clever. In fact, she was a witch; and when she bewitched anybody, he very soon had enough of it; for she beat all the wicked fairies in wickedness, and all the clever ones in cleverness. She despised all the modes we read of in history, in which offended fairies and witches have taken their revenges; and therefore, after waiting and waiting in vain for an invitation, she made up her mind at last to go without one, and make the whole family miserable, like a princess as she was. So, she put on her best gown, went to the palace, was kindly received by the happy monarch, who forgot that he had forgotten her, and took her place in the procession to the royal chapel. When they were all gathered about the font, she contrived to get next to it and throw something into the water; after which she maintained a very respectful demeanour till the water was applied to the child’s face. But at that moment she turned round in her place three times, and muttered the following words, loud enough for those beside her to hear: ‘Light of spirit, by my charms, Light of body, every part, Never weary human arms – Only crush thy parents’ heart!’ They all thought she had lost her wits and was repeating some foolish nursery rhyme; but a shudder went through the whole of them notwithstanding. The baby, on the contrary, began to laugh and crow; while the nurse gave a start and a smothered cry, for she thought she was struck with paralysis: she could not feel the baby in her arms. But she clasped it tight and said nothing. The mischief was done.

steps.text: Managing children's questions

steps.editorState:
• Money is a sensitive subject.
  • All families have different ideas about what they want to talk to children about.
  • These activities are designed to start conversations - but it is up to you to decide what to tell children.
  • Children are curious - and have no idea that some questions might be too personal.
  • There is no need to talk about anything you don't want to.
  • This may be a good opportunity to teach them how to talk about money politely and sensitively.
  • Asking a question back can be a good way to return the conversation back to them.

Deflecting tricky questions

It can sometimes be tricky when children ask question that you don't feel comfortable answering.

Here are some possible responses:

Q: How much money do you have?

How much money people have is usually something they keep private.  

It's also quite complicated for grown ups - it changes all the time so there isn't a simple answer.

Adults bank accounts can also be complicated. You can have different accounts for different things.

We have enough money for what we need.  

Questions to ask back:

  • What do you think adults need to pay for with their money?  
  • Do you know how much money you have in your money box? 
  • Can you think of good ways to keep track of how much money you have?
  • Why do you think adults keep money in bank accounts and not in money boxes?

Q: How much do you earn?

People's salaries are often private. Exact amounts are not something people usually share.  

When you are talking to people, they may think it was rude to ask them about how much they earn.  

There isn't one number to say how much you are paid as money is taken off for Tax and Pensions and National Insurance and Student loan payments before you even get it.

I earn more now than I did when I worked at . . because I have more responsiblity and have to work at the weekends more.

I earn less now that I did when I worked at . . but I have more time at home with you and don't have to travel as far.

Questions to ask back:

  • What kind of job would you like to do? Why?
  • Which do you think will be more important to you - salary, a good work-life balance or doing a job you enjoy?

steps.text: How do maths games help with learning?

steps.editorState:
Fun

Games can be an enjoyable, motivating way to practice a skill many times.

Positive feelings

Having fun together encourages positive feelings towards maths and can reduce worry about making mistakes.

Memory

Skills that are practiced when a child is fully engaged and relaxed are more likely to be remembered.

Number sense

In trying to win, children really think about the numbers they choose. This builds number sense - a deeper, more flexible understanding of numbers.

Problem solving

Finding strategies to win develops problem solving skills.

Mathematical Vocabulary

Talking about a game or explaining it to someone else encourages children to use mathematical vocabulary.

Deeper thinking

Changing a rule and talking about how that impacts a game encourages an even deeper level of thinking.

steps.text: How to make your own letters

steps.editorState: You will need at least 26 things to write your letters on. If you have more, that will be good because some words have the same letter more than once, but don’t worry too much – 26 is a good number to start with!

What could you write letters on?

  • Pieces of card cut from a cereal box
  • Milk bottle lids
  • Large, dried beans, e.g. butterbeans
  • Wooden pegs
  • Small pebbles
  • Anything you like, as long as you can write on it and your child can move it around to make words!

What should I write with?
A permanent marker like a sharpie would work well. On wooden pegs, an ordinary pen or felt tip will also work fine.

What letters should I write?
The full alphabet in lower case.

  • If you have some spares, the capital letter that starts your child’s name.
  • If you have more spares, extra letters for any that are in your child’s name more than once.
  • If you still have spares, keep some blank in case your child asks for something in particular.

details.name: Alliterating names
details.nameForContentDev: Alliterating names for who's in the bag

steps.editorState:
Too tricky?

Take it in turns to describe a person from the bag without using the timer. This is a bit more of a relaxing way to play, with no winner or loser at the end.

How to play:

  1. Start the timer.
  2. Player 1 takes a name out of the bag.
  3. Player 1 describes the person to player 2. 
  4. Player 2 must try to guess the person.
  5. When Player 2 guesses correctly, Player 1 starts describing the next person.
  6. Keep describing until the time runs out.
    • Any names that have not been guessed when the time runs out should be put back in the bag. 
    • Player 1 (the person describing) should keep all the names that were correctly guessed.
  7. Swap over so that Player 2 can describe.
  8. Keep swapping until all the names have been guessed.
  9. The winner is the player with the most names collected at the end of the game.

Setting up:

  1. Think of fictional or famous people whose first and last names start with the same letter, e.g. Helga Hufflepuff.
  2. Write a name on each piece of paper. 
  3. Fold each name in half and put it in your bag.

When you are shopping it is useful to add up the cost as you go.

To make this easier, you can round each price to the nearest pound.

Rounding Reminder:

If the price has 49p or less (0.49), round down.

If the price has 50p (0.50) or more, round up.

Extra Challenge:

  • Make a list of 3 or more prices.
  • First, round them to the nearest pound and add them.
  • Then, add them exactly.
  • How close is the rounded estimate?

What to do:

1. Look at some prices.

(They could be in a shop, on a receipt or just made up)

2. Round each to the nearest pound.

3. Practice until you can do this easily.

steps.text: M X L made from pencils.

steps.editorState:
What to do:

  • Roll the dice (or write some numbers on paper and put them in a bowl)
  • Work together to make or write the number in Roman numerals.
  • Or make it competitive - who can make it first?

Roman Numbers Reminder

I - 1

V - 5

X - 10

L - 50

C - 100

D - 500

M - 1000

Extra Challenge:

Ask other members of your family for their date of birth.

Write their years in Roman numerals.

What to do:

Now write the year you were born in Roman numerals.

Warm up:

Read the Roman numerals together.

Work out when these famous people were born?

Did you know:

Until the 16th Century, Roman numbers were used in Britain.

Shakespeare's father would have used Roman numbers.

Then Roman numbers were replaced by the Arabic numbers 0-9.

steps.text: A cartoon of a koala dressed as a roman soldier.

steps.editorState:
What to do:

Try these Roman number calculations.

  • XXII + XV
  • Half of CXXXVI
  • Double XIX
  • XXI multiplied by X

Discussion:

How did you find calculating with Roman numbers?

What was easy? What was hard?

Why do you think people switched to Arabic numbers?

There is no zero in Roman numbers. Why is zero useful?

steps.text: Tricky to move around?

steps.editorState:

  • Count up in 5s
  • Count up in 10s
  • Count up in 2s
  • Count up in 20s
  • Count up in 25s

What to do:

  • Take 100 steps - counting as you go.
  • You could guess where you will get to before you start.
  • Then make a 100 from different moves.
  • Maybe 10 jumps, then 10 hops, then 10 skips . . 
  • Or 5 claps, 5 hops, 5 jumps . .

steps.text: How to make bubble mixture

steps.editorState:
What can we use as a bubble wand?

Here are some ideas:

What to do:

  1. Measure the washing-up liquid into your container. 
  2. Slowly add the water, being careful not to make too many bubbles yet!
  3. Gently stir the mixture.
  4. Ideally, let the bubble mixture rest before you use it.

You will need:

  • 50ml washing-up liquid
  • 300ml water
  • A large bowl for mixing
  • Something to stir with - a chopstick or spoon will work well
  • Measuring jug or weighing scales

How to play:

Just blow the bubbles and play!

Encourage your child to:

  • Get down low or reach up high: Wow! You jumped so high!
  • Grab the bubbles with their hand: I wonder if you can catch the bubbles?
  • Pop them with a finger: Point and POP! Point and POP! 

ALL of these big and small movements are strengthening your child’s muscles and helping their balance and coordination!

steps.text: How to make bubble mixture

steps.editorState:
What can we use as a bubble wand?

Here are some ideas:

What to do:

  1. Measure the washing-up liquid into your container. 
  2. Slowly add the water, being careful not to make too many bubbles yet!
  3. Gently stir the mixture.
  4. Ideally, let the bubble mixture rest before you use it.

You will need:

  • 50ml washing-up liquid
  • 300ml water
  • A large bowl for mixing
  • Something to stir with - a chopstick or spoon will work well
  • Measuring jug or weighing scales

carouselData.textEditorState:
Putting on our space boots, suit and helmet

Make the movements needed to put these things on our bodies.

Taking off in a rocket

Countdown 5-4-3-2-1... then blast off into space and run really fast on the spot until you reach the moon.

Going for a moonwalk

Make big slow steps lifting your feet up really high.

Spinning planets

Turn around slowly with your arms out – try not to get too dizzy!

Twinkling stars

Wiggle your fingers and thumbs like twinkling stars.

Back down to earth

Gently glide through the atmosphere as you slowly walk around and land safely sitting on the floor.

steps.text: How does this help?

steps.editorState:
Going on a space walk together helps children to:

  • Have fun while being physically active and developing their strength and co-ordination;
  • Become aware of the positions of their bodies in relation to objects around them (‘spatial awareness’);
  • Learn new words as they play.

steps.editorState:
How to play:

You can play this game anywhere – at home, on the bus, on the way to the shops, or even at the shops! 

  • Start with just a few basic shapes – a square, a circle or a triangle.
  • When you spot a shape, take a bit of time to look at it carefully – name it, and if you can, trace round the edges, perhaps counting the sides – all these things will help to develop your child’s early maths skills.
  • Take some photos of the shapes you find to look at together later and chat about what you remember about the shapes you’ve discovered.

steps.text: How does this help?

steps.editorState:
Going on a shape hunt will help your child to: 

  • Practise their early maths – recognising and naming shapes, counting how many they find, etc.
  • Learn new words – names of shapes.
  • Have something to focus on – it helps with their attention, makes the walk more fun and encourages you to chat together.
  • Improve their observation and memory – can they remember what all the square things were?

steps.text: A coordinate grid drawn on paper with axes in all 4 directions from the zero.

steps.editorState:
How to play:

  1. Player 1 says a coordinate.
  2. Player 2 checks their grid.
  3. If there is a turtle there, Player 2 ticks it and says 'turtle'.
  4. If not, Player 2 says 'splash'.
  5. Swap over, so Player 2 says a coordinate.
  6. Players should mark the squares they have tried so they don't repeat.
  7. The winner is the first one to locate all 5 of the other player's turtles.

Finding coordinates tricky

  • Just draw the axes with positive numbers.

steps.text: The same coordinate grid with 5 green blobs to represent turtles.

steps.text: How does this help?

steps.editorState:
Cuddling up together with a story can be a very special time – a time where:

  • You can your child can enter into a shared world, where they can explore and learn safely;
  • Your child can ask questions about things that puzzle or worry them – this helps them to understand and deal with their fears;
  • Their imagination can run free;
  • New language and meanings can be explored;
  • You can laugh and have fun together!

details.name: How does sharing a book help?

carouselData.textEditorState: Let your child turn the pages.
Point out things in the pictures that you notice, or that are spoken about in the words of the story.
Try changing your voice as you read, or make noises or movements to go with the characters or the pictures.
Chat together about what you see, and wonder what might happen next.
Turn off any background noise (e.g. TV or music) so your child can focus on sharing the book with you.

steps.editorState:
You can share a book anywhere! At home, on the bus, at the park, waiting at the doctors or the dentist.

steps.text: How do I find a library?

steps.editorState:
What if there is no library near me?

Some areas also have a mobile library, which provides all the same services as an ordinary library branch but can move around to different places that don't have a physical library. You can find their routes and timetables online.

Alternatively, Children's Centres and Family Hubs often have books that can be borrowed - or you could ask at your child's nursery!

Search ‘libraries’ on google maps to find libraries near you.

You can also enter your postcode on the gov.uk website to find your nearest library.

steps.text: Colourful boxes of books at a children's library.

carouselData.textEditorState: There are so many different kinds of books to borrow and look at together.
It’s a friendly, cosy place to pop into when you’re out shopping or need a change of scene.
A library is good place for a rest with a tired or bored toddler!
Many libraries have a story and rhyme-time – sometimes even a Peep session if you’re lucky!
Some have activities after school or at the weekends for older children, and often events in the holidays.
Libraries are not just for children - they offer useful services for adults too.

  6. You can add your own information as well.

One million years ago:

The earth was colder than it is now and there were frequent ice ages.

The UK was connected to Europe by land.

Early humans were using fire and tools.

There were many different reptiles and birds.

There were wooly mammoths and sabre toothed tigers.

There are no dinosaurs - they've been dead for 64 million years.

  • A ruler
  • Earth timeline fact sheet printed or on screen.

steps.editorState:
There are different ways to work these out.

You may find different methods work best for different examples.

Counting up:

You can count up in steps until you reach 1 million.

50,000 . . .100,000 . . .150,000 . . .. 

Use a known fact:

I know there are 1000 thousands in 1 million.

So there must be five 200s in a thousand.

There must be five thousand 200s in a million.  

Division:

1,000,000 divided by 200 is 5,000

How to play:

  1. Player 1 draws the main character at the start of the page.

Extra Challenge:

  • What is the smallest number of dice rolls you could win in?
  • Which numbers do you need to roll for this?
  • Which numbers do you need to roll to land on 12.

You'll need.

  • Paper and pens.
  • A 0-20 number line drawn for each player.
  • A dice - or use the one below.

What to do:

  1. Each player starts at 20.
  2. Player 1 rolls the dice.
  3. They subtract number on the dice, drawing jumps.
  4. Player 2 rolls the dice.
  5. They subtract the number on their number line.
  6. The winner is the first player to reach zero exactly.
  7. If you roll a number that would go past zero, wait until your next turn and try again.

Finding it tricky:

  • Use a number line to 10.
  • Place a counter or small item on each number on the line.
  • Take items away as you subtract instead of drawing jumps.

steps.editorState:
What to do:

Create a giant number line.

You can choose how high the numbers go.

  • You could write numbers on pieces of scrap paper.
  • You could cut up cardboard boxes.
  • You could peg numbers on a washing line.
  • You could chalk numbers on the ground.

Then:

  • Ask each other adding and subtracting questions.
  • Step along the number line to answer.
  • For example: 7+3 or 9-6.

To make this more challenging:

  • Use larger numbers.
  • Make your questions a story using First, then, now.

For example. First there were 7 bees on the flowers. Then 3 flew away. How many are there now?

  • Ask 'secret number' questions.  

I started on a secret number, added 5 and I landed on 8. What's my secret number?

What to do:

  1. Player 1 tells a simple story using the toys.
  2. Using 'first, then, now' can help.
  3. For example: First there were 8 bears on the bus, then 3 got off and now there are 5.
  4. Player 2 writes this as a number sentence: 8+3=11
  5. Then swap over.
  6. Try and do some stories with addition and some with subtraction.

You'll need:

  • A few toys.
  • Pencil and paper.

steps.text: Four soft toys

Extra Challenge:

  • Add another 'then' stage to your story.
  • For example: First there were 4 bears on the bus, then 3 got on, then another 2 got on.
  • As a number sentence this is: 4+3+2=9

This activity involves making number toys for children to play with.

It will take a bit of time to make, but will hopefully last a few weeks.

Playing with them for a few minutes at a time will really help children understand and enjoy number sentences.

steps.editorState:
What to do:

  • Write the numbers 0 to 10 and +,-,= individually on small items.
  • Children may enjoy helping to make these.
  • Leave them out for children to play with and make number sentences.

Extra Challenges:

  • How many sentences can you make with the answer 5?
  • Or make a sentences yourself with a missing number
  • For example: 4+ . . .=6.
  • Ask children to put the missing piece in.
  • Challenge children to use all 3 symbols. For example 4+1=7-2.

Finding it tricky:

  • Place small items like pasta or lego bricks under each number.
  • For example, for 3+4 place 3 items under the number 3 and 4 under the number 4.

How to use the part-whole model.

steps.editorState:
Example 1:

Working out the missing number in 5+?=12

  1. Count out 12 counters.
  2. Put them in the big circle.
  3. This is the whole.
  4. Count 5 of these into the smaller circle.
  5. This is one part.
  6. Move the rest of the counters to the other small circle.
  7. This is the other part.
  8. Count them to find the missing number.

Example 2:

Working out the missing number 12-?=3

  1. Count out 12 counters. 
  2. This is the whole.
  3. Place them in the bigger circle.
  4. Move counters one at a time into the smaller circle until there are 3 left.
  5. 3 is a part.
  6. The number you have moved is the other part.
  7. Count these to find your missing number.

steps.editorState:
How to play:

First, Player 1 is the Maths machine.

They decides an action.

For example: +2 or -3.

They keep this secret.

They can write it down if they want to.

The aim of the game is for Player 2 to guess what the maths machine is doing.

Then, Player 2 says a number

Player 1 does their action and says the answer.

Player 2 says another number.

Player 1 does the action again and says the answer.

After that, Player 1 guesses the action.

Swap roles and play again.

Extra Challenge:

  • Add some more possible actions to the game.
  • For example doubling the number or halving the number.

This is a more challenging game.

Play it when children are confident adding and subtracting numbers in their heads.

How to play:

Some of your bugs are going on a school. You must check if you have an odd or even number to see if they will be able to walk in pairs!

  1. Put all the bugs into your bag.
  2. Take out a handful of bugs.
  3. Have you got an odd number or an even number of bugs? How do you know?

steps.editorState:
Here are the song words:

One, two, buckle my shoe;

Three, four, knock at the door;

Five, six, pick up sticks;

Seven, eight, lay them straight;

Nine, ten, a big fat hen;

Eleven, twelve, dig and delve;

Thirteen, fourteen, maids a-courting;

Fifteen, sixteen, maids in the kitchen;

Seventeen, eighteen, maids in waiting;

Nineteen, twenty, my plate's empty.

In this song, each line has two numbers. 

  • The first is odd. 
  • The even number is part of the rhyme. 

Can you spot the even numbers and the words they rhyme with?

What to do:

Odd and even numbers are used for different things. If you spot some when you are out an about, stop to talk about them. You could ask your child what they notice about the numbers and decide together whether they are odd or even.

How to play:

  1. Player 1 chooses a letter of the alphabet. Player 2 is going to try to work out what it is.
  2. Player 1 asks a question that has a one-word answer.
  3. Player 2 answers the question with one word.
  4. Player 1 says "good" or "bad":

    • Bad: the one-word answer does not contain the letter.

  6. Keep asking and answering questions until Player 2 is ready to guess the letter. If they guess correctly, they win. If they don’t, Player 1 wins.

What to do:

  • Look at the different types of data on the carousel.
  • Is it continuous? This means the data is changing all the time.
  • Is it discrete? This means the data is a number that can be counted. 
  • Line graphs are used for continuous data.

steps.text: Types of data explained.

steps.editorState:
Discrete data 

This is data that can be counted.

It is usually whole numbers.  

There isn't meaningful information between the numbers.

For example: The number of cats each house in a street has. Any whole number of cats is possible but you can't have half a cat!

Discrete data can be shown in bar charts, pictograms and pie charts.

Continuous data

This is data that is changing continually.

It is measured at intervals rather than counted.

There is meaningful information between the points that are measured

For example - a child's height can be measured every year. The child is growing slowly between these measurements. You can estimate the child's height halfway between measurements.

Continuous data can be shown in line graphs.

steps.text: The calculations below written individually on scraps of paper
Tips on choosing a strategy

steps.editorState:
Column addition is useful when:

  • Carrying is required

For example 8237+1879

Column addition is probably not the best strategy when . .

  • Only one column changes

For example: 4567+300.

  • A small number is being added

For example: 2997 + 14

Here it would be easier to add 3 to make 3000 and then add 11.

  • A number could be rounded and adjusted

For example: 3440 +4999

Easier here to add 5000 and take one from the answer.

  • No carrying is required.

For example: 4231+3215.

The thousands, hundreds, tens and ones can be added together easily.

Choosing when to use column addition is really important.

Sometimes informal methods are much easier.

details.name: Choosing a strategy
details.nameForContentDev: Year 4 Column addition tips for strategies

steps.text: Soda bread recipe

steps.editorState:
Method:

  1. Preheat the oven to 180°C/350°F/gas 4. 
  2. Squeeze the lemon juice into the milk. Stand to one side for about 5 minutes to allow the liquid to curdle and separate. 
  3. Meanwhile, weigh the flour into a bowl, add the bicarbonate of soda and mix through. 
  4. Make a well in the centre of the flour and pour in most of the milk-and-lemon mixture. Mix well with a wooden spoon to form a sticky dough. Use your judgement – if it looks too dry, add the remaining liquid. 
  5. Tip the dough on to a floured work surface and pat into a round shape, kneading ever so lightly. The trick to amazingly light soda bread is not to fiddle with it too much. 
  6. Pop the shaped dough into the loaf tin, score a line on top of the dough down the middle about 1cm deep with a sharp knife and dust with a little extra flour. 
  7. Place in the preheated oven for 40 minutes. 
  8. Once baked through, the loaf should sound hollow on the bottom when tapped and feel ridiculously light. 
  9. Remove the tin from the oven, tip out the soda bread whilst hot and leave to cool on a wire rack. 
  10. Break into chunks and serve warm with butter, or allow to cool completely then wrap in cling film to keep fresh.

Ingredients:

  • Juice of ½ a lemon or 2 teaspoons bottled lemon juice
  • 300ml milk
  • 400g self-raising flour plus extra to shape the dough and dust the loaf
  • 1½ level teaspoons bicarbonate of soda

by Jack Monroe

Makes 1 small loaf that will serve 6

Equipment:

  • Two bowls
  • Measuring spoons
  • Wooden spoon
  • 1lb loaf tin (approximately 17 x 7 x 6cm) 
  • Sharp knife (for adult use)
  • Cooling rack

Challenge:

Choose one of these other lists. Think about which thing is the odd one out and some reasons why, then think about all the other things in the list and give reasons why they could be the odd one out instead!
Some things you might have said

Here are some things you might have said:

  • Horse because:
    • it’s the only one you’d find running in the Grand National;
    • it’s the only one that could also describe how your voice sounds when you have a sore throat.


  • Cow because:
    • it’s the only one people don’t usually ride;
    • it’s the only one which also describes the female of its species;
    • it’s the only one that can also be a verb – to make someone do what you want by intimidating them, e.g. “The king had cowed his people into silence.”


  • Donkey because:
    • it’s the only one that has another noun (key) inside it;
    • it’s the only one you can ride on at the seaside.


  • Camel because:
    • it’s the only one isn’t usually found on farm in the UK;
    • it’s a zoo animal not a farm animal;
    • it’s the only one which is also a colour.


  • Mule because:
    • it’s the only one I hadn’t heard of before;
    • it’s the only one that’s a cross between two other animals – it’s the offspring of male donkey and a female horse;
    • It’s the only one that is also the name of a type of shoe.


  • Pony because:
    • it’s the only one that’s a small version of one of the others;
    • it’s the only one which is a slang term for an amount of money (£25).

A good strategy here is to bridge through a multiple of 10.

Some children may be able to do this in their heads.

Some children may still need to use a number line.

To be able to do use this strategy, a child needs to know:

Tips:

  • You could make up a theme tune.

  • Talk about what the other person is doing, a bit like a narrator.

steps.text: Which animals should I cross?

steps.editorState:
You can choose any two parent animals you like. Here are some ideas:

  • Two similar animals, e.g. two different breeds of dog.
  • Two more different animals, e.g. a lion and a tiger.
  • Two totally different animals (this might be a bit fantastical), e.g. a tortoise and a flamingo.

Activity 1 - Physical jumps to 100 - ie 56, 4 small steps to 60 then big steps for 10s to 100. 

Activity 2 - Tens and ones on the table.   

Numberline challenge

Activity 2 Change in shops - imagine you have a £1 what change will you get.

What to do:

  1. Player 1 rolls the dice below (or says any 2 digit number).
  2. Player 2 uses jumps to work out how many to 100.
  3. Do small jumps for 1s until you get to a multiple of 10.
  4. Then do big jumps for 10s
  5. If moving around is tricky, use a toy to do the jumping.

For example:

  • Player 1: "64"
  • Player 2 jumps in 1s: "65,66,67,68,69,70" "That's 6 ones jumps"
  • Then in 10s "80,90,100" "That's 3 tens jumps"
  • "It's 36"

Finding it tricky?

  • Start with multiples of 10.

Number bonds to 100 can help calculate change.

100p is the same as £1.

What to do:

  1. Label some items with prices under £1.
  2. Take it in turns to be the customer and shop assistant.  
  3. The shop assistant has to work out the change from £1.
  4. You could also do this in a real shop.

A line drawing of a £5 note
How to help children work this out

steps.editorState:
Calculating mentally.

Some children may go straight to calculating in their heads.

One way to do this is to . .

  • Make the tens add up to 9
  • Make the ones add up to 10.

steps.text: Items that can be used as tens and ones including chocolate fingers and raisins, pens and lids, spaghetti and pasta.

steps.editorState:
For example:

If the price is 64p.

Count out 'ones' until you get to 70.

There should be 6.

Then count out 'tens' until you get to 100.

There should be 3.

You now have 3 tens and 6 ones.

The answer is 36.

This is what shop keepers used to do with coins before electronic tills.

It was called 'shop keepers addition'.

• Using real objects can help children visualise the calculation.
  • Choose objects to represent tens and ones.
  • You'll need 9 of each.
  • If you have enough 10p and 1p coins use those for extra money practice.
2) Using tens and ones:

1) Using a number line:

  • Start with the price.
  • Make small jumps in ones until you reach a multiple of 10.
  • Make big jumps in tens until you reach 100.
  • The total jumps show the change.
Children may find one of these approaches useful when calculating the number bond.
